Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 winners by court ruling

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1681 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sadio Mane's Senegal have been confirmed as Afcon 2025 winners following their appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, giving the Teranga Lions a second continental title.
  • Senegal have been reinstated as winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations after a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport.
  • The court's award overturns a previous decision which had stripped the West Africans of the title they won on the pitch during a chaotic final against host nation Morocco in January.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sadio Mane's Senegal have been confirmed as Afcon 2025 winners following their appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, giving the Teranga Lions a second continental title.

Senegal have been reinstated as winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations after a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

The court's award overturns a previous decision which had stripped the West Africans of the title they won on the pitch during a chaotic final against host nation Morocco in January.

According to recent reports, with the game goalless, Senegal left the field of play in second-half stoppage time in protest at a penalty awarded against them. The match in Rabat was delayed by over 15 minutes before Morocco's Brahim Diaz had his spot-kick saved.

Senegal then triumphed 1-0 after extra time, with Pape Gueye scoring the winner.

That result was overturned almost two months later when a Confederation of African Football (Caf) appeals board decreed the Teranga Lions had breached competition regulations by leaving the field of play after the penalty was awarded.

Senegal's football federation (FSF) subsequently appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), sport's highest legal authority, with a three-man panel hearing its case behind closed doors in Lausanne on 8 October.

In a recent development, in a unanimous verdict, the Cas panel has effectively backed the decision by referee Jean-Jacques Ndala to restart the game after Senegal returned to the field and the match was played to a conclusion. The result of the final stands and Senegal are now confirmed as Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) 2025 winners.

A statement issued by Cas said the court considered that "the referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority".

"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met - both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume.".

The FSF immediately reacted with a social media post featuring a picture of the side lifting the trophy in January captioned with the phrase "again and always champions of Africa".

"The FSF welcomes this ruling with deep satisfaction," it later said in a statement.

"This decision affirms, above all, the triumph of sporting fairness and reaffirms a fundamental principle: the true outcome of a match is determined exclusively on the field of play, under the protection of sports law.".

Meanwhile, Morocco's football federation (FRMF) expressed "surprise" at the ruling and added that it would "pursue all available legal avenues to challenge the decision".

Caf is yet to comment but its president Patrice Motsepe has repeatedly remarked that his organisation will respect and adhere to the Cas ruling.

The full grounds for the decision will be published by Cas in due course unless the parties request confidentiality.

'Shameful' and 'terrible look' - the chaos that marred Afcon 2025 final.

'The longest VAR check in history' - the fallout from shock Afcon decision.

Senegal's walk-off during the final in Rabat has already brought about a change in football's rules.

"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at â a âreferee's decision," stated Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, in April.

"This upcoming rule will also apply âto any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match âto be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match.".

Morocco and Senegal have both changed coach since the Afcon 2025 final and earlier this month secured their places at the 2027 edition of the tournament with two rounds of qualification remaining.

Referee Ndala was at the centre of the controversy during the Afcon final.

A tightly contested final between the continent's top-ranked sides produced two moments of controversy in second-half stoppage time, with referee Ndala at the centre of the drama.

First the Congolese official denied Senegal a near-certain goal, blowing his whistle for a challenge by Abdoulaye Seck on Morocco right-back Achraf Hakimi moments before Ismaila Sarr nodded in.

The free-kick looked soft, but the video assistant referee (VAR) was unable to get involved because Ndala had awarded the foul before the ball crossed the line.

Three minutes later came a flashpoint in the Senegal box, when El Hadji Malick Diouf tugged Morocco playmaker Diaz back before heading a corner clear.

Diaz vehemently claimed a penalty and Ndala eventually awarded a spot-kick after being sent to consult his pitchside monitor by the VAR.

Senegal coach Pape Thiaw called his players over to the touchline, and Thiaw subsequently headed down the tunnel to the changing room in protest against the decision - accompanied by several players.

They eventually returned, but over 15 minutes had elapsed since the award of the penalty by the time Real Madrid's Diaz failed to convert, with his Panenka-style attempt easily saved by goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.

Meanwhile, there was unrest inside the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium as a small contingent of Senegal supporters clashed with security staff.

The game went into extra time, with midfielder Gueye scoring the goal which settled the contest in Senegal's favour.

Off the pitch, another match involving disciplinary boards and lawyers would soon begin.

Brahim Diaz's penalty was saved by Edouard Mendy after Senegal's walk-off led to a delay of over 15 minutes before he was able to take the spot-kick.

Senegal celebrated their second continental title but the FRMF rapidly lodged an appeal with Caf, arguing their opponents had breached Article 82 of Afcon regulations, which covers withdrawals.

It states that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" it shall be "considered [the loser] and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition".

A disciplinary board from the continental game's governing body rejected the FRMF's appeal days after the final as it sanctioned and fined those found guilty of unsporting conduct during the match.

Yet in March, almost two months on from the final, a Caf appeals board ruled that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarded Morocco a 3-0 victory.

The FSF described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and swiftly lodged its case with Cas.

The director general of the Switzerland-based court remarked arbitration proceedings would be conducted "as swiftly as possible", but it was over five months until all parties descended on Lausanne for a one-day hearing.

The Cas panel was led by Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.

Both the FRMF and FSF were able to nominate an arbitrator to exercise an independent judicial function once their appointment was confirmed.

Sources indicate that the FRMF nominated Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli, while the FSF nominated Hamburg-based attorney and professor of âlaw at the University of Zurich Ulrich Haas. Those two men completed the Cas panel.

Over six weeks on from that hearing - and 10 months since the Afcon 2025 final - Senegal have been proclaimed champions once again.

But the debate and damage done to the reputation of African football is likely to linger for some time yet.

Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 winners.

In its appeal, the FSF argued that the decision of referee Ndala to resume the match in the 19th minute of added time - and to allow it to be concluded with a sporting result - could not be reviewed, pursuant to the 'field of play' doctrine.

Cas has a long-standing practice where it refrains from "reviewing decisions taken on the playing field by referees for applying the rules of the game, unless there is evidence that those rules were applied arbitrarily or in bad faith".

The FRMF argued, on the contrary, that the referee's decision did not fall under the field of play doctrine because Senegal should have faced disciplinary consequences for walking off the pitch.

The Moroccan federation went on to argue that, according to Afcon tournament rules, the referee should have brought the match to an early conclusion.

It added that Ndala "erred in law" and that his decision was "arbitrary".

However, in the view of the panel, the referee's decisions were limited to the pitch and the relevant Afcon regulations regarding withdrawals were not applicable.

"The panel acknowledged that the referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension," the Cas statement added.

It has been revealed that "However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as 'arbitrary'. On the contrary, the referee's judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game.".

Court of Arbitration for Sport reinstates Senegal as Afcon winners.

Despite Cas being the highest authority in sport, and its decision coming 10 months on from the final, there could yet be a further twist.

The FRMF raised a grievance with the process before the panel's judgement was announced on Tuesday.

It alleged that German attorney Haas, the arbitrator on the panel nominated by the Senegalese, held a telephone call with FSF president Abdoulaye Fall on Sunday.

Fall "categorically" denies that any such phone call ever took place.

The FRMF indicates that any unauthorised communication between a member of the panel and one of the interested parties would constitute a serious breach of Cas regulations.

It has demanded that "appropriate legal consequences be applied to actions that compromise the integrity and credibility of the arbitration process".

The Moroccans could appeal against the ruling by taking the case to the Swiss Federal Tribunal, and the country's highest court could set Cas' judgement aside.

The case would then likely be heard again at Cas, with a different panel in place.

A precedent would be the case of Chinese swimmer Sun Yang, who had an appeal against the decision by Cas to impose an eight-year doping ban upheld by the Swiss Federal Tribunal.

A new panel heard his case at Cas, and his ban was reduced to four years and three months.

'Star Trek: First Contact' at 30: Resistance is futile when it comes to the 'Next Generation' crew's greatest massive-screen adventure

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Following the sad news of Sir Patrick Stewart's passing, there's been no shortage of discussion about his best moments as Captain Jean-Luc Picard.
  • With the Borg overrunning the newly launched USS Enterprise-E, Picard — who has long-standing beef with the Collective, following his assimilation in classic "The Next Generation" story "The Best of Both Worlds" — orders his crew to fight the cybernetic nasties hand-to-hand if required, defying their pleas to activate the ship's self-destruct system and retreat.
  • But following some impassioned talk about making the Borg "pay for what they've done", he's finally talked down from his rage by 21st-century stowaway Lily Sloane (Alfre Woodard).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following the sad news of Sir Patrick Stewart's passing, there's been no shortage of discussion about his best moments as Captain Jean-Luc Picard. "The Inner Light"'s life in 25 minutes is a strong contender, as are the courtroom grandstanding in "The Measure of a Man" and his insistence (under extreme torture) that "there are four lights!" in "Chain of Command". But for this writer's money, it's hard to look past a nine-minute sequence in "Star Trek: First Contact", which turns 30 this weekend.

With the Borg overrunning the newly launched USS Enterprise-E, Picard — who has long-standing beef with the Collective, following his assimilation in classic "The Next Generation" story "The Best of Both Worlds" — orders his crew to fight the cybernetic nasties hand-to-hand if required, defying their pleas to activate the ship's self-destruct system and retreat. He even calls Worf — not a man renowned for dodging a fight — a coward, prompting the Klingon to respond that, "If you were any other man, I would kill you where you stand." Ouch.

But following some impassioned talk about making the Borg "pay for what they've done", he's finally talked down from his rage by 21st-century stowaway Lily Sloane (Alfre Woodard). She points out that his Moby-Dick-esque obsession is on the verge of going full Ahab, and he eventually sees sense, issuing the order to abandon the Enterprise and destroy the hive.

Sources indicate that it's a masterclass showcasing the ever-brilliant Stewart's impressive range, as the out-of-control captain's rarely seen temper reaches fever pitch, before normal service is resumed. His subsequent apology to Worf — "As a matter of fact, I think you're the bravest man I've ever known" — is simply perfect.

Industry observers note that and just as the franchise's zenith, "The Wrath of Khan", is built around Kirk and Khan's decades-old feud, "First Contact" is precision engineered to get the most out of Jean-Luc. This was the right "Star Trek" at the right time, a film that put "TNG"'s greatest villains on a collision course with the origins of Starfleet. It's not quite "Khan", of course — what is? — but it deserves to be mentioned in the same breath.

In 1996, the "odd numbers bad, even numbers good" rule of "Trek" films still, more or less, rang true. 1994's "Generations", rushed out a few months after "The Next Generation" ended its seven-year run on TV, had done decent business, but the seventh movie's convoluted "passing the baton" storyline had left many fans cold. Now, however, with Kirk killed off, it was time for Picard and his crew to explore the big-screen frontier alone.

Recent findings suggest that william Shatner actually pitched a resurrection storyline for Kirk, but "Trek" executive producer/overlord Rick Berman ruled that it was a little too soon to bring the good captain back. Instead, he hired "Generations" scripters and "TNG"/"Deep Space Nine" writers' room regulars Brannon Braga and Ronald D. Moore to craft an eighth movie capable of living up to its even-numbered predecessors.

According to recent reports, while "Generations" had been written to an extremely restrictive brief, Braga and Moore were given much more freedom the second time out. Berman was keen on a time-travel storyline while Braga lobbied for the fan-favorite Borg, and early on they explored the idea of taking the Collective back to Renaissance Italy. These plans were abandoned when Stewart vetoed the idea of wearing tights.

They eventually zeroed in on April 5, 2063, the date Zefram Cochrane (a character who'd previously appeared in Original Series episode "Metamorphosis") made humanity's first warp flight and put Earth on the radar of a passing Vulcan ship.

"We landed on the idea of what I called the 'Star Trek' nativity scene — the birth of 'Star Trek'," Braga said in "The Fifty-Year Mission" by Mark A Altman and Edward Gross.

"The three wise Vulcans who arrive on Earth and step out of their ship for our first contact with an extraterrestrial species. And the Borg were going to prevent that from happening, which really struck a bullseye for me, because it would allow non-'Star Trek' people to understand why 'Star Trek' matters by putting the crew and the Borg back in that time frame. I thought it would appeal to a larger audience. 'Star Trek' itself was at stake, and that was super cool to me.".

Industry observers note that paramount reportedly flirted with big-name directors like Ridley Scott ("Alien", "Blade Runner") and John McTiernan ("Predator", "Die Hard"), before settling on Jonathan Frakes. Although this would be Frakes' first movie, the man best known for playing Commander Riker had directed numerous "Trek" episodes. Berman believed that an understanding of the franchise's DNA was more important than big-screen experience.

Recent findings suggest that the film wastes little time on exposition for "Trek" newbies, with just a short dream sequence to explain away Picard's history with the Borg. With a single Borg Cube on course for Earth, the Federation fleet mobilizes to fight them off. They're getting their asses well and truly kicked, too, until the Enterprise warps into the battle.

Recent findings suggest that the Cube is ultimately destroyed but still manages to dispatch a Sphere, which uses chronometric particles to travel back to 2063 in order to assimilate Earth in the past. Picard has no choice but to follow them back to "repair whatever damage they've done".

They arrive in a post-World War III Montana, where Cochrane has constructed his prototype faster-than-light vessel, the Phoenix. Played by "Babe" star James Cromwell (who'd already guest-starred in a trio of "TNG" episodes), Cochrane is some way from the man future history has remembered: a hard-drinking womanizer more motivated by potential riches than the betterment of mankind. A man uncomfortable with the idea that a high school will one day bear his name.

But as some of the crew work to repair the damage caused by the Sphere's bombing raid, there are bigger problems in orbit. Borg survivors have beamed on board the Enterprise and started assimilating the vessel and its crew.

Initial drafts of the script saw Riker leading the ship-based resistance while Picard remained on Earth, but — at Stewart's request — Braga and Moore flipped things round to bring the captain face-to-face with his nemesis. It proved to be a really smart move, as Stewart got to ditch his new-look Starfleet uniform and run around the Enterprise as a full-on action hero in a John McClane-style vest.

These Borg had been given a multiplex upgrade, with massively improved prosthetics and upcoming extendable tendrils that injected nanoprobes to assimilate a victim from within. Frakes played up the horror aspects of the Collective, portraying them as a horde of mindless cybernetic zombies, while using "Alien" and "Aliens" as inspiration.

Sources indicate that "[Ridley Scott and James Cameron] made it clear that when it comes to villains, the more that's suggested, the scarier they are," Frakes explained. "I tried to get that with the Borg.".

The biggest change came at the head of the organization, where — at the suggestion of Paramount executive Jonathan Dolgen — "First Contact" introduced a previously unseen Borg Queen (brilliantly played by Alice Krige) to act as spokesperson for the Collective.

It has been revealed that bringing a singular entity to a civilisation built on the notion that there's no "I" in "team" was a controversial move, but it made perfect dramatic sense. Indeed, a legion of drones would have little chance of seducing Data, even if it was just for 0.68 seconds.

It has been revealed that "We wrestled with it quite a bit before we committed to [the Borg Queen's] character," Moore told Syfy Wire, "because it was a choice that was also antithetical to the idea of the Borg. The whole concept of these villains was that they were a collection, and that there were no individuals. And that's what made them the faceless, implacable 'resistance is futile' enemy. But it also limited how to deal with them dramatically because it meant that any scenes you always had to deal with this sort of collective voice. We decided that the story would be better if we had some individual to deal with.".

The Queen was also granted one of the greatest entrances in sci-fi history, as her head and torso were lowered into a robot body with a bit of help from Industrial Light & Magic.

The Starfleet armada's assault on the Borg was similarly impressive and effectively a test run for "The Phantom Menace", as ILM's visual effects supervisor John Knoll pioneered the CG effects pipeline that would later become pivotal to the "Star Wars" prequels. It was also a brilliant excuse to introduce several new starship designs to the "Trek" canon.

Sources indicate that they're standout moments in a film that made the most of its comparatively puny budget of $45 million (reported). (For comparison, "Independence Day", which was released the same year — and also featured Brent Spiner — cost closer to $75 million.).

As Moore later recalled in an interview with the Hollywood Reporter, "Paramount had their formula. They said that 'Star Trek' movies only make this amount of money. So, therefore, you can only have this amount of budget to make it. And, at that point, we were still — just like on the TV show — counting phaser beam effects shots [to keep the price down].".

It has been revealed that the studio needn't have worried. "First Contact" was a huge hit with fans and became one of the franchise's highest-grossing films at the box office. Borg mythology introduced here (including the Queen) would become a mainstay on "Star Trek: Voyager", while Jean-Luc would get to face his cybernetic white whale again in "Picard" — though the incomparable Stewart arguably never again had another "Trek" scene to rival the ones he had here.

"Fortunately it happened to be a wonderful script, and my job was not to screw it up," mentioned Frakes. "It also holds up as a movie that just happens to be a 'Star Trek' movie, which we were all hoping would be the case.".

'Star Trek: First Contact' is available to stream on Paramount+ in the US and the UK.

Industry observers note that richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor.

According to recent reports, he's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nike stated Tuesday ahead of its first investor day in nine years that it was reaffirming its 2027 financial guidance.
  • It has been revealed that the retailer also laid out a financial framework and said that by the end of fiscal 2031 it's targeting approximately $5 billion in incremental revenue growth from fiscal year 2027, operating margins of 12% to 14% and adjusted earnings per share of $3.00 to $3.50.
  • Nike's 2027 financial guidance includes expectations for revenue to decline in the high-single-digit range, an adjusted operating margin of approximately 6%, and adjusted EPS of $1.15 to $1.35.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nike stated Tuesday ahead of its first investor day in nine years that it was reaffirming its 2027 financial guidance.

It has been revealed that the retailer also laid out a financial framework and said that by the end of fiscal 2031 it's targeting approximately $5 billion in incremental revenue growth from fiscal year 2027, operating margins of 12% to 14% and adjusted earnings per share of $3.00 to $3.50. The firm said higher-quality revenue, gross margin expansion and productivity improvements would help it reach its goals.

Nike's 2027 financial guidance includes expectations for revenue to decline in the high-single-digit range, an adjusted operating margin of approximately 6%, and adjusted EPS of $1.15 to $1.35.

The manufacturer also introduced a strategy it's calling Full Stride Ahead, which the company stated aims "to get closer to athletes and focus resources on the greatest opportunities for long-term growth.".

Nike CEO Elliott Hill told CNBC's Sara Eisen that the newly introduced initiative is about "being closer to the athletes we serve.".

"What's different today is the depth and breadth we're taking from an innovation perspective," Hill said.

He added that Nike is emphasizing sportswear at a time when sports have never been more relevant around the world. Hill also remarked Nike is working to regain its cultural relevance, after a perceived dropoff contributed to its slowdown both in its home market and in China.

Nike said it would focus on performance sports and sportswear opportunities "with the greatest potential for long-term growth," and said its five priority sports would be running, training, global football, basketball and outdoor.

Nike is holding an investor day at its Oregon headquarters Tuesday as the company aims to prove to investors that its turnaround strategy is yielding success after a yearslong slump.

According to recent reports, last month, the company reported mixed fiscal first-quarter results as it unveiled a restructuring proposal, including layoffs that it said would start next year. It's the company's third round of layoffs to be announced this year.

Nike's net income and revenue both fell during the most recent period compared with a year ago, and the company said it expects revenue to decline by a high single-digit percentage in fiscal 2027.

The newly introduced strategy, dubbed Pace, focuses on the manufacturer's supply chain and reorganizing into three geographies. Nike said the turnaround plan is expected to deliver roughly $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031.

Sources indicate that nike has been seeing significant sustained declines in its China market, where revenue last quarter dropped 26%. Experts have remarked the manufacturer is losing relevance in the country, while Nike has said it's actively working to win over younger consumers.

In a recent development, at the same time, Nike revealed last quarter that it's creating a upcoming global campus in India as part of its new growth strategy, hoping the country will help boost its performance. The company mentioned it was remaining focused on China even as it begins to build out its India presence.

Nike COO Venkatesh Alagirisamy told CNBC the tech giant sees an opportunity to triple its business in the country over the next five years.

He added that Nike's broader strategy will position it for success in India.

"If you look at the three components, brand building, landing those innovations into marketplaces in an increasingly locally connected fashion and then doing all of those things in a much faster pace really aligns well with the aspirations for India," he remarked.

CEO Elliott Hill's turnaround strategy includes improving different parts of the business at different rates based on priority. While it's seen some signs of progress in the North America business, Hill has said that performance isn't enough to offset the pressures on the company elsewhere, including internationally.

The Nike consumer has also been under increased macroeconomic pressure as geopolitical tensions mount and inflation rises.

Shares of Nike have fallen 50% over the past two years.

A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal.
  • Recent findings suggest that to investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal.
  • Recent findings suggest that the experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal. Known as a heavy fermion state, this phenomenon causes electrons to behave as though they have much greater mass than normal. These states are associated with extraordinary quantum effects, including unconventional superconductivity, and the discovery could provide a latest way to develop materials with unusual electronic properties.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal. They then used powerful synchrotron light to study the electrons and their interactions at the boundary between the two materials. The results showed that electrons confined to the thin atomic layer could interact with freely moving electrons in the copper beneath it, producing the unusual heavy fermion behavior.

Two Distinct Quantum States Emerge.

Recent findings suggest that the experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics. One existed primarily within the two-dimensional atomic layer, while the other reached beyond that layer and into the three-dimensional copper crystal below.

The second state was particularly important because it provided the first direct evidence of heavy fermion behavior generated by interactions across such an interface. Researchers traced the effect to the mixing, or hybridization, of localized ytterbium 4f electrons in the atomic layer with mobile conduction electrons inside the copper substrate. This interaction demonstrated how combining materials with different electronic characteristics can produce quantum behavior that neither material would necessarily exhibit on its own.

"This achievement was made possible by our continued efforts to create high-quality materials and measure their electronic states as precisely as possible," claims senior author Professor Shin-ichi Kimura. "Our next goal is to engineer and control such heavy-electron states, opening the way to previously unexplored quantum states, including unconventional superconductivity.".

A Newly introduced Approach to Designing Quantum Materials.

The discovery suggests that the boundaries between materials could become powerful tools for creating and controlling exotic quantum states. Rather than relying only on the properties of individual substances, scientists may be able to develop entirely new electronic behaviors by carefully selecting and combining ultrathin atomic layers with suitable underlying materials.

Future research could focus on adjusting the structures of these interfaces, controlling the electronic orbitals involved, and manipulating moiré patterns that arise when atomic arrangements overlap. Such approaches may allow researchers to produce and fine-tune quantum phenomena in materials with extremely small dimensions, including effects that cannot be achieved in conventional materials. Ultimately, this could open new possibilities for engineering advanced quantum materials and investigating unconventional superconductivity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.

Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.

His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, unveiled his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”.

Brathwaite’s work has been the subject of resurgent interest from curators, historians and collectors in recent years, and his first major institutional retrospective, which was organized by the Aperture Foundation, made its debut in 2019 at the Skirball Cultural Center in Los Angeles before touring the country.

Brathwaite was born in 1938 to Barbadian immigrants, in what he referred to as “the People’s Republic of Brooklyn” in New York, though his family moved from there to Harlem and then to the South Bronx when Brathwaite was 5 years old. He attended the School of Industrial Art (now the High School of Art and Design) and, according to profiles of Brathwaite in T Magazine and Vice, was drawn to photography by two moments. The first was in August of 1955, when a 17-year-old Brathwaite encountered David Jackson’s haunting photograph of a brutalized Emmett Till in his open casket. The second was in 1956, when — after he and his brother Elombe co-founded the African Jazz Arts Society and Studios (AJASS) — Brathwaite saw a young man taking photos in a dark jazz club without the use of a flash, and his mind became alight with possibility.

According to recent reports, using a Hasselblad medium-format camera, Brathwaite attempted to do the same, learning to work with limited light in a manner that enhanced the visual narrative of his imagery. He would soon also develop a darkroom technique that enriched and deepened how Black skin would appear in his photography, honing the practice in a small darkroom in his Harlem apartment. Brathwaite went on to photograph jazz legends performing throughout the 1950s and ’60s, including Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Thelonious Monk and others.

“You want to get the feeling, the mood that you’re experiencing when they’re playing,” Brathwaite told Aperture Magazine in 2017. “That’s the thing. You want to capture that.”.

A 106-year-old from the Philippines is Vogue's oldest ever cover model.

By the early 1960s, alongside the rest of AJASS, Brathwaite began using his photography and organizing prowess to consciously push back against whitewashed, Eurocentric beauty standards. The group came up with the concept of the Grandassa Models, young Black women whom Brathwaite would photograph, celebrating and accentuating their features. In 1962, AJASS organized “Naturally ’62”, a fashion show held in a Harlem club called the Purple Manor and featuring the models. The show would go on to be held regularly until 1992. In 1966, Brathwaite married his wife Sikolo, a Grandassa Model whom he had met on the street the year prior when he asked if he could take her portrait. The two remained married for the rest of Brathwaite’s life.

By the 1970s, Brathwaite’s focus on jazz shifted to other forms of popular Black music. In 1974, he traveled to Africa with the Jackson Five to document their tour, also photographing the historic “Rumble in the Jungle” boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman in what’s now the Democratic Republic of Congo that same year. Commissions in this era also saw Brathwaite photographing Nina Simone, Stevie Wonder, Sly and the Family Stone, Bob Marley and other music legends.

Creating for community: The Black designers placing identity and heritage at the center of their brands.

Recent findings suggest that throughout the ensuing decades, Brathwaite continued to explore and develop his mode of photography, all through the lens of the “Black is Beautiful” ethos. In 2016, Brathwaite joined the roster of Philip Martin Gallery in Los Angeles, and he was continuing to photograph commissions as recently as 2018, when he shot artist and stylist Joanne Petit-Frère for The Latest Yorker.

T Magazine’s 2021 profile, published on the occasion of Brathwaite’s retrospective traveling to the Blanton Museum of Art in Austin, Texas, noted that the photographer’s health was failing such that he was unable to be interviewed for the article. A separate exhibition, “Kwame Brathwaite: Things Well Worth Waiting For,” is currently on view at the Art Institute of Chicago, where it will remain until July 24.

#173675. Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1264 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1264 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, an eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function.
  • In a recent development, the findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time.
  • Industry observers note that the discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, an eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.

In a recent development, the findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.

Industry observers note that the discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.

Industry observers note that these questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.

To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills.

One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

Recent findings suggest that cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.

The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.

"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently.

The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.

In a recent development, among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.

Sources indicate that working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing latest information.

Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.

The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.

Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity.

According to recent reports, the study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.

Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.

One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.

This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.

"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

Sources indicate that "However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is notable to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing.".

What the Eight-Year Study Revealed.

The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.

According to recent reports, the current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.

Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.

To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.

Sources indicate that importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.

Nevertheless, the results offer an key perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.

The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.

Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.

The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

Though there’s room for disagreement about which catastrophe is most salient, experts are aligned on the idea that society is, for one reason or another, in real trouble. This begs one big question: What are industry leaders doing to mitigate the danger they’ve unleashed? Though a pause in training models, a data center moratorium, and other regulation has been proposed, the industry hasn’t exactly made changes that are putting people at ease around AI safety. Meanwhile, critical infrastructure seems more and more vulnerable every day. We’re gathering our Backchannel team, who will deploy their expertise on the ins and outs of Big Tech and AI safety, to answer all your questions.

That timing is meant to line up with the iOS/macOS 27.4 upgrade cycle, at which point Gurman notes we could also see the iPhone 18 and 18e models, a new OLED iPad Air, and a new budget iPad.

According to recent reports, apple upgrading a laptop just a year after release is not unheard of. In recent years, the company has been releasing annual upgrades of its MacBook Air and Pro lines, outfitting the devices with the latest Apple Silicon, sometimes with few other changes.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

As for what to expect from the new MacBook Neo, it doesn't sound like a hugely substantial upgrade at this point in time. From a usability standpoint, the most important thing Gurman mentioned is that the A18 Pro chip powering the original Neo will be upgraded to an A19 chip, with RAM bumped from 8GB to 12GB as well.

According to recent reports, it remains to be seen if the current $699 starting price for the MacBook Neo will go up, but it's definitely a possibility. We do live in a RAMageddon world, after all, and Apple has already raised the price of the Neo once. It's also worth pointing out that the A19 chip powering the Neo 2 would still be less capable than the M-series chips powering more expensive Mac computers. Even the upcoming iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have an A20 Pro chip.

Beyond the chip improvement, Apple is also looking to add fresh MacBook Neo colors "frequently," per Gurman. However, Gurman didn't say for certain whether or not that will start with the second iteration of the budget laptop. On this day in space! Nov. 21, 1676: Danish astronomer discovers speed of light — by accident — while observing Jupiter's moon Io

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (467 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Space

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of light.
  • Rømer disproved this almost by accident when he was studying Jupiter's moon Io.
  • To his surprise, the timing of the eclipses was not consistent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of light. Before Rømer figured it out, scientists thought that light travels instantaneously, or infinitely fast.

Rømer disproved this almost by accident when he was studying Jupiter's moon Io. He was trying to figure out how long it takes Io to orbit Jupiter in hopes of using it as a cosmic clock. He watched Io disappear behind Jupiter and reappear on the other side. He did this over and over every 42 hours for years.

To his surprise, the timing of the eclipses was not consistent. When Earth was closest to Jupiter, the eclipses happened 11 minutes early. Likewise, when the two planets were farthest away, the eclipses were 11 minutes behind schedule.

Rømer figured out the pattern and made an accurate prediction for Io's eclipse on Nov. 9, 1676. Then on Nov. 21, he took his findings to the Royal Academy of Sciences and explained that a finite speed of light must be responsible.

Understanding that the speed of light is a constant is the key that opened our ability to gauge the scale of the universe, as well as was central to developing modern physics."The speed of light becomes a sort of ultimate speed limit," Live Science explained in an article about why the speed of light matters. "In fact, objects with mass, be they cars or neutrinos, can't reach the speed of light because they would need infinite energy to do so.".

Latest Update: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (777 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism.
  • The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal key differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
  • The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism. Although adults with and without autism demonstrated remarkably similar brain activity when researchers compared group averages, a closer examination uncovered striking differences between individuals. These differences were especially pronounced in brain regions involved in understanding and responding to social information.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal key differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The discovery could help scientists better understand why autism varies so widely from person to person and eventually support more personalized approaches to care.

The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.

What Brain Scans Reveal When People Watch Movies.

To explore these differences, the team examined previously collected brain imaging data from Indiana University and Caltech. The recordings captured brain activity as adults with and without autism watched movies from several genres, including animation, action, romantic comedy, and Hitchcockian thrillers.

It has been revealed that movies offered researchers a way to study how the brain responds to a constantly changing stream of sights, sounds, and social interactions. Unlike simple laboratory tasks, movies present a rich mixture of information that more closely resembles the complexity of everyday experiences.

Using the imaging data, the researchers trained a computational model to identify connections between brain activity and different elements of the movies. These included visual details, sounds, and more abstract social information, such as interactions between characters.

After training, the model was able to accurately predict activity across several brain systems.

Kliemann explained why this approach is particularly useful for investigating the social challenges sometimes associated with autism: "The computational model allowed us to look for robust brain responses to many different aspects of the complex, dynamic contexts in the movies.".

A Surprising Difference Hidden by Brain Activity Averages.

The most unexpected finding emerged when researchers compared the two groups.

At first, the results suggested relatively little difference. When brain responses were averaged across participants, the model predicted activity in various brain systems similarly for adults with and without autism.

However, the picture changed when the researchers examined how much individual participants differed from others in their own group.

It has been revealed that people with autism showed substantially greater variation in their brain responses than participants without autism. In other words, although the overall group averages looked similar, the responses of individual autistic participants were much less alike.

In a recent development, this increased variability appeared across nearly every brain system examined. The strongest differences occurred in the social brain system, a network of regions involved in processing social information and understanding other people.

Why the Findings Could Change Autism Research.

It has been revealed that the results raise key questions about how scientists investigate autism. Many existing approaches to understanding and treating the condition rely heavily on comparing average measurements from groups of autistic and nonautistic individuals.

But if autistic people show considerable differences in how their brains process information, these averages may obscure some of the most meaningful findings.

Recent findings suggest that traer described the team's surprise: "We were surprised by the similarity of group averages. The results suggest that we need to focus on understanding the details of individual brain responses. How and why do they differ?".

Rather than searching only for brain activity patterns shared by everyone with autism, the findings point toward the potential value of studying individuals and identifying smaller groups with similar characteristics.

Kliemann highlighted what this could mean for future research and support: "Identifying ASD subgroups may help us build a more precise understanding of the condition and help develop ways to provide individually tailored support.".

The researchers now plan to investigate how these differences in brain activity relate to variations in autism-related behavior. They hope to determine where and when the differences emerge, how they are connected to individual characteristics, and what might explain them.

Ultimately, the findings suggest that understanding autism may require looking beyond the average brain and paying closer attention to the distinctive ways individuals process the world.

Tech Report: Study finds slightly higher risk of autism diagnosis in areas with more lithium in drinking water, but experts say more research is needed

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 5 min read (973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.
  • About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
  • Scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.

About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder. Genetics may be a factor, but some have been looking at potential environmental causes, too.

Autism diagnosis has become more common, but pandemic disrupted early detection, CDC states.

It has been revealed that cases may be on the rise, but that is also unclear. One study published this year on cases in the Upcoming York-New Jersey area found that autism diagnosis rates tripled among certain age groups between 2000 and 2016. A 2021 report found similar increases in cases, but the CDC claims the increased number of cases is most likely linked to more doctors screening for the condition.

Lithium is an alkali metal that can be found naturally in some food and ground water. It’s used in batteries, grease and air conditioners, as well as in the treatment of bipolar disorder and some blood disorders. Its levels in US drinking water are not regulated, according to the US Geological Survey.

A upcoming study, published Monday in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, found a small association between lithium and autism diagnosis in Denmark, where the researchers say the level of lithium in drinking water is similar to that in American water systems.

The researchers checked a database of people with psychiatric disorders for children born between 2000 and 2013 to find information on 8,842 cases of ASD and 43,864 participants who did not have ASD. They then measured the concentration of lithium in 151 public waterworks that served more than half of the Danish population and mapped out where pregnant people lived in relation.

For many neurodiverse people, 'The Sims' has been a lifelong comfort.

According to recent reports, as lithium levels in water increased, there was a modest increased risk of an ASD diagnosis. Specifically, compared with people at the lowest exposure level, those who had the second and third highest exposure during pregnancy had a 24% to 26% higher risk of ASD diagnosed in children. The group with the highest exposure had a 46% higher risk than those at the lowest level of exposure.

The researchers could not tell how much water the pregnant people drank, but they picked Denmark in part because residents there consume some of the lowest amounts of bottled water in Europe.

Experts say it’s important to note that the research can’t show that lithium exposure leads directly to an autism diagnosis.

Further study is required, noted study co-author Dr. Beate Ritz, a professor of neurology in the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and a professor of epidemiology and environmental health at the UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

“Any drinking water contaminants that may affect the developing human brain deserve intense scrutiny,” Ritz remarked in a news release. She added that the research would need to be replicated in other countries to look for a similar connection.

The implications of the findings are complex as far as public health policy is concerned, according to an editorial published alongside the study. Lithium levels in water, at concentrations that the study associated with a potential ASD risk, have also been linked with health benefits such as lower rates of hospitalization for psychiatric disorders and suicide.

In a recent development, “If all these of associations are valid, the wisdom of Solomon will be required to develop guidelines for lithium in drinking water that are maximally protective of the entire population,” wrote Dr. David C. Bellinger, a professor of neurology and psychology at Harvard Medical School. “Until the basic biology of ASD is better understood, it will be difficult to distinguish causal from spurious associations.”.

'Heartbreaking' delays in autism diagnosis and treatment got even worse during pandemic.

Dr. Max Wiznitzer, director of the Rainbow Autism Center at University Hospitals Rainbow Babies and Children’s Hospital in Cleveland, points to other research on the effects of lithium on pregnant people who take it for mental health disorders. Those studies – which look at people exposed to much higher levels than are found in drinking water – do not show a connection with autism spectrum disorder.

“It’s an interesting association, but causation is definitely not proven,” said Wiznitzer, who was not involved in the new research. “We have to see if there’s a viable and biologically plausible mechanism by which a small amount of lithium in the water supply can somehow do this, yet pharmacologic dosing of lithium in women with bipolar disorder has not been reported to be causing increased risk of ASD.”.

Other studies have also suggested connections between ASD and environmental exposures to things like pesticides, air pollution and phthalates. But none of them points to any of these factors as a direct cause of the disorder.

A link between environmental exposure and ASD is hard to prove, Wiznitzer stated. With research showing that increased exposure to air pollution raises the risk of giving birth to a child with ASD, for example, he often wonders whether pollution is the determining factor or if it’s just the populations who live in more polluted areas.

In a recent development, “There’s a lot of speculation about about environmental factors, but how many of them are truly causally associated?” Wiznitzer remarked. “We are bombarded with a variety of environmental stressors in our everyday lives. We have to figure out how to basically safely navigate them, and this is probably not one that’s high on our list.”.

RIIZE brought their online fandom into the real world. I was there to see it.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1861 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • That was one of my first thoughts on Friday night as I watched K-pop group RIIZE perform for roughly 600 fans at Brooklyn Steel in New York City.
  • Industry observers note that it's a funny contradiction, considering the entire premise of the evening was to bring digital fandom into the physical world.
  • The occasion was Spotify CLOSER, a upcoming live music series that brings artists and their most dedicated listeners together for intimate performances and conversations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We need to bring back MTV Unplugged.

That was one of my first thoughts on Friday night as I watched K-pop group RIIZE perform for roughly 600 fans at Brooklyn Steel in New York City. There were no elaborate stage productions or arena-sized crowds. Instead, there were stripped-down performances, candid conversations, a few wonderfully awkward moments, and a sea of smartphones held high above the audience.

Seriously, everyone had their phones out.

Industry observers note that it's a funny contradiction, considering the entire premise of the evening was to bring digital fandom into the physical world. But maybe that's just what being a fan looks like in 2026. Even when we're standing a few feet away from our favorite artists, we still want to capture the moment, preserve it, and inevitably share it with everyone who couldn't be there.

The occasion was Spotify CLOSER, a upcoming live music series that brings artists and their most dedicated listeners together for intimate performances and conversations. After launching in Seoul in Oct., the series made its U.S. debut on Nov. 20 with RIIZE, bringing together more than 600 fans from the New York tri-state area, many of whom were identified as the group's top local listeners and selected based on their listening habits.

It has been revealed that since debuting under SM Entertainment in 2023, RIIZE — consisting of Shotaro, Eunseok, Sungchan, Wonbin, Sohee, and Anton — has emerged as one of K-pop's most prominent fifth-generation acts, performing at major festivals like Austin City Limits and Lollapalooza South America. But despite their growing international popularity, the group has only toured the U.S. once, making opportunities for American fans to see them in person relatively rare.

For many, their relationship with RIIZE has largely unfolded online, through music, livestreams, social media, and the seemingly endless stream of content that makes K-pop fandom feel like a full-time commitment.

In other words, the same platform that connected these fans to RIIZE's music was now bringing them face-to-face with the six people behind it. And I was curious to see what would happen when that connection moved offline.

Before RIIZE even took the stage, Spotify had transformed Brooklyn Steel into something of a playground for BRIIZE, the group's devoted fandom.

In a recent development, there was a fisheye photo station, branded Spotify x RIIZE microphone keychains, and an area where fans could write letters to the members. Nearby, six lockers offered a glimpse into each member's personality, decorated with objects representing their individual interests.

Shotaro's locker featured a camera and bucket hat, while Eunseok's included boxing gloves and a Doraemon plushie. Sungchan's was outfitted with a soccer ball and cleats, and Wonbin's displayed Nike Air Force 1s and earbuds. Sohee's locker featured a Boston cap and Naruto figures, while Anton's contained a violin and swimming goggles. Each member had also written a personal letter to BRIIZE.

According to recent reports, for longtime fans, these weren't just random objects. They were familiar details, the kinds of things you pick up from watching livestreams and behind-the-scenes content. You can know an idol's favorite foods, recognize their sense of humor, and feel familiar with their friendships without ever having met them. Seeing these details arranged in physical space felt a little like stepping inside the digital world fans had spent years getting to know.

And that was the interesting thing about the event. Spotify wasn't simply bringing fans closer to RIIZE by putting them in a smaller room. It was recreating the familiarity of online fandom in a setting where fans could participate, leaving their own messages alongside the members' handwritten notes.

Of course, once RIIZE appeared, nearly every phone in the room went up, mine included. So much for going offline.

Recent findings suggest that the crowd was enthusiastic and eager to interact, with handwritten signs scattered throughout the audience. My personal favorite was a sign directed at Anton that simply read, "Slap me." (I have questions, but I respect the commitment.).

Anton, who grew up in Newly introduced Jersey, received particularly enthusiastic cheers from the Garden State contingent. There was also a very important geography lesson in which fans informed the members that Peter Parker, aka Spider-Man, is from New York. You know, the essential cultural exchange that happens when a K-pop group visits the city.

These were the kinds of interactions that made the evening feel less like a conventional concert and more like a gathering of people who already knew one another, even if most of them had never actually met.

And for RIIZE, it was an opportunity to put faces to the streaming numbers.

RIIZE opened the night with "Get A Guitar," their 2023 debut single, performed entirely in English for the first time. The setlist also included "Boom Boom Bass," "Impossible," "D-D-Done," "Love 119," and the first U.S. performance of "Do your dance.".

But the evening wasn't just about the music. Between performances, the members participated in a Q&A hosted by Anton, who served as the group's unofficial emcee and occasional English translator. He kept the conversation moving, prompting his bandmates to answer questions and helping bridge the language gap with the predominantly English-speaking audience, while live subtitles appeared on the screens.

Sources indicate that initially, the members seemed a little reserved. Away from the familiar structure of a performance or the carefully edited chaos of variety content, there was a certain shyness to their early exchanges, as though they were still finding their footing in a more spontaneous setting.

Sources indicate that but as the Q&A progressed, that initial hesitation gave way to something more playful. The members began teasing one another, laughing more freely, and engaging with the crowd. Sohee, in particular, seemed to come alive as the night went on. Funny, expressive, and naturally charismatic, he grew increasingly comfortable commanding the room, revealing a different side of the confidence he already brings to the stage as one of the group's standout vocalists.

It was fun to watch that transformation happen in real-time.

It has been revealed that during one segment, the members voted on which of them best fit a series of superlatives. Sungchan was named the funniest, Anton earned the title of biggest flirt, and Shotaro received a unanimous vote for best smile. The conversations were sometimes silly, occasionally awkward, and all the more charming for it.

My favorite exchange came when Shotaro was expressing his appreciation for the fans. After delivering a heartfelt message, he earnestly added, "Please forget that.".

Anton was quick to correct him: "Please don't forget that.".

According to recent reports, that small moment captured the easygoing charm of the night. RIIZE are a group accustomed to the precision of rehearsed performances, but here, in front of hundreds of fans, they were navigating something far less predictable. There was no choreography to fall back on, no script for a misplaced word or an unexpected laugh. Just six guys figuring it out together, and letting their personalities shine in the process.

For all the playful banter and fan interactions, the moment that stayed with me most was RIIZE's performance of their newly introduced single, "Insomnia.".

Industry observers note that the song is already one of the group's more understated offerings, performed without choreography, but for Spotify CLOSER, RIIZE took that intimacy a step further with a new, even more stripped-down arrangement. The performance put the focus squarely on their voices, allowing their harmonies to shine and giving the song a different kind of emotional weight. There was something lovely about hearing a song that was already relatively restrained given even more room to breathe.

It was the closest the evening came to the spirit of MTV Unplugged, the iconic music series that invited artists to reinterpret their work in a more intimate setting.

In a recent development, that's not to say RIIZE needed to abandon the choreography or elaborate performances that are so integral to K-pop. But there's something special about hearing artists approach their own material from a different perspective, especially when it brings out details that might otherwise go unnoticed.

Watching "Insomnia," I found myself missing that kind of music programming — the opportunity to see artists experiment with familiar songs, to hear their voices in a new context, and to experience a performance that feels entirely specific to a particular room and moment.

Sources indicate that spotify CLOSER isn't quite Unplugged, nor does it need to be. But the appeal feels similar. Sometimes, hearing a familiar song in a different way is enough to make you appreciate it all over again.

There's a certain irony in a streaming platform creating an event designed to bring fans away from their screens. Especially when nearly everyone in the room was holding up a phone.

In a recent development, spotify CLOSER is, of course, a branded experience. It's a way to reward highly engaged listeners while creating exclusive content that can eventually circulate on the platform. Select performances from the evening will be released on Spotify, allowing fans around the world to experience some of what happened in Brooklyn.

In a recent development, but the commercial nature of the event doesn't make the connection any less meaningful. If anything, the night illustrated how intertwined our digital and physical experiences of fandom have become.

The fans at Brooklyn Steel didn't leave their online identities at the door. They brought their phones, their handwritten signs, their knowledge of the members' personalities, and all the inside jokes and shared references they'd accumulated from following RIIZE online. And the members, who initially seemed a little timid, gradually relaxed into the kind of playful, slightly clumsy interactions fans have come to love through their screens.

As the evening drew to a close, RIIZE expressed their hopes of returning to New York before ending with an encore performance of "One Kiss.".

For all the ways technology has made artists more accessible than ever, there's still something it can't quite replicate: the spontaneity of sharing a room, where a mistranslated word can become a joke, a fan's sign can spark a conversation, and a familiar song can sound entirely latest.

And for the record, Shotaro, I won't forget that.

Latest Update: Nvidia Is Powering Brain-Computer Interfaces Now

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (716 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A Michigan woman named Mary has a chip in her brain roughly the size of a dime.
  • According to recent reports, made by brain-computer interface manufacturer Paradromics, the implant is outwardly invisible, but the speech decoding requires a cart full of electronics.
  • Today, Austin-based Paradromics declared a partnership with the AI chipmaker to use Nvidia’s hardware and software to process its brain data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A Michigan woman named Mary has a chip in her brain roughly the size of a dime. Though she struggles to speak due to motor neuron disease, the implant allows her to express her thoughts through a synthesized voice on a computer.

According to recent reports, made by brain-computer interface manufacturer Paradromics, the implant is outwardly invisible, but the speech decoding requires a cart full of electronics. A year from now, however, that cart will be transformed into a small box that can sit on her wheelchair, thanks to technology from Nvidia. Eventually, those electronics will be so small they’ll fit in a phone, claims Paradromics CEO and founder Matt Angle.

Today, Austin-based Paradromics declared a partnership with the AI chipmaker to use Nvidia’s hardware and software to process its brain data. Nvidia is facing a major leadership shakeup and federal scrutiny following longtime CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Sources indicate that though Mary has lost much of the use of her speaking muscles, neurons in her brain still fire when she attempts to speak. The Paradromics implant uses more than 400 embedded electrodes to capture those signals, and a computer uses artificial intelligence to make inferences about what she’s trying to say. The words appear on a screen, and the computer speaks the words for her.

That decoding process takes an incredible amount of computing power. The cart of electronics has to be plugged into an electrical outlet, and Mary must be within range of the cart in order to use her brain-computer interface.

According to recent reports, “We're producing a huge amount of data that has a lot of value, but we need to translate that neural data into applications in order to make this a really effective platform,” Angle claims. It’s why he calls brain-computer interfaces the ultimate case for edge computing, a distributed computing model that processes and stores data in physical devices close to where it is generated rather than sending it to a distant cloud or data center.

“We want to be able to do it through increasingly smaller and lower-power devices, and the people leading in that area are Nvidia,” he states.

Making brain-computer interfaces practical and portable for patients is a major challenge for the field. While these setups have become far more streamlined since their early days in academic labs, they still require lots of external electronics. Shrinking them down and reducing their power requirements would allow patients to be more mobile with these devices, using them wherever they go.

Paradromics aims to do that by using Nvidia’s Jetson, a low-powered computing module that will allow speech decoding to be done in a small device close to the user. It will also use Holoscan, Nvidia’s AI sensor processing software, to allow owners to interact with computers and other devices with low lag time. Brain-computer interfaces will need to work alongside other sensors, such as cameras and microphones, and Holoscan will help process these different data streams together so applications can respond to both neural signals and the context around them.

“Brain-computer interfaces must translate complex neural signals into meaningful actions in real time. Even small delays can make communication feel unnatural,” David Niewolny, Nvidia’s director of business development for health care and medical, tells WIRED via email. “Neural signals also change over time, requiring AI that can continuously adapt to the individual.” Nvidia’s technology processes neural signals and runs AI models in real time.

Reducing lag time is important for a brain-computer interface with a speech function so that users can have naturally flowing conversation without delays.

Industry observers note that through the partnership, Paradromics will also be able to integrate Nvidia’s foundation models into its brain-computer interface. Vikash Gilja, chief scientific officer at Paradromics, says AI models could help make synthesized voices more expressive and human-like. Also, if these models are running locally on Nvidia hardware, it means customers won’t have to be connected to the internet in order to use their devices.

Niewolny claims he sees “tremendous potential for AI to expand human capability.” Nvidia is working with other players in the brain-computer interface space, including Synchron. The chipmaker will not have access to brain data through these partnerships, he says.
