"Star Trek: First Contact" celebrates its 30th anniversary today, and the engaging sci-fi classic still looks fantastic three decades later. With the sad passing of its star, Patrick Stewart, last month, and "Star Trek's" milestone 60th birthday taking place in 2026, this is a bittersweet salute that also holds an extra special significance.

Directed by "The Next Generation's" Number One, Jonathan Frakes, in his feature film debut, "First Contact" consistently ranks as one of the finest "Star Trek" feature films among fans and critics, and those accolades are well deserved.

Industry observers note that based on a compelling screenplay by Brannon Braga and Ronald D. Moore, "First Contact" remains as bright and beautiful as ever, brimming with bravado, heart, horror, and heroism.

In a recent development, not only was it a bona fide crowdpleaser when it was released by Paramount over Thanksgiving week on Nov. 22, 1996, but it was also a financial success for the studio, eventually pulling in a worldwide total of $212 million off a modest $45 million budget.

Honestly, who can forget Alice Krige's seductive Borg Queen, Marina Sirtis’ Deana Troi tipsy on tequila, Brent Spiner's Data feeling the sensation of human skin, Patrick Stewart’s Jean-Luc Picard reliving past traumas, and James Cromwell's Zephram Cochrane blasting off in the Phoenix and dancing to Roy Orbison's "Ooby Dooby"?

Recent findings suggest that we caught up with Frakes for "First Contact's" 30th anniversary to hear why this "Trek" treasure holds up and warp back to Hollywood’s heyday of the '90s. Resistance is futile!

"What’s not to love?" Frakes tells SPACE regarding the film’s lasting popularity. "It was bulletproof. Dean Devlin ["Stargate," "Independence Day"] and I have very similar sensibilities about filmmaking. We like the whole idea of action, adventure, comedy, and in the case of 'First Contact,' a little horror as well. ILM’s John Knoll, the guy who won the Oscar for 'Star Wars,' just happened to be our Special Effects Supervisor.".

"First Contact" is filled with memorable moments and indelible performances, some of which certainly stand out for Frakes looking back over the years on the production.

"The two things that always come to mind were the beautiful scene with Alfre [Woodard] and Patrick, the Moby Dick scene, where she claims, 'You broke your little ships,'" he recalls. "I was sitting under the camera with my face in my hands, watching two heavyweights go at it take after take. It was what you dream of. They were into it. The writing was great. We had time to do it right, and they were fabulous together.

"That and the Cromwell and Marina drunk on tequila scene. It's not only one extended take, but it contributes to the pace of the movie in the right kind of way. My wife tells me that I was really good in that scene because I was exhausted and relaxed. It’s true, you’re exhausted when you’re filming and acting at the same time. I got to sit there and watch those two. It was like watching a tennis game.".

Many Trekkies might not know that Alfre Woodard is Frakes' godmother, and he had specifically asked producer Rick Berman for approval to include her in the movie’s cast.

Industry observers note that "She's one of our finest American actors," he notes. "Rick stated, 'If we can get Alfre, that would be great.' I knew she’d do great with Patrick, so that was a no-brainer. I never had a godmother, and when I came out here to live in LA back in 1979, an old friend from college, Nathan Cook, was working with Alfre. We were at a barbecue, and it came up. She said, 'You don’t have a godmother? I’ll be your godmother.' I asked what that meant, and she said, 'I’ll be in charge of your spiritual being.' It's been a magical friendship that turned into her playing that part.".

The hive-minded cybernetic collective known as the Borg featured prominently in the time-travel tale, and that second filming unit did a masterful job lighting those scenes.

In a recent development, "The Borg costumes were torture, from what I was told," says Frakes. "We had our own set of ADs and an entirely separate special effects makeup crew, and the costume department had a certain number of Borg to build and rebuild. Now the Borg had been on the show, but with these Borg we had more time and more moving parts. It was kind of an enhanced thing that really paid off. I look back so fondly on that entire experience. Also, the Borg were one of the great movie villains. They held up!".

Frakes couldn’t be prouder of "First Contact", and he reminds us that most people like it right next to 1982's "Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan." That's rarefied air indeed!

According to recent reports, "We got Cromwell coming off of 'Babe.' So we had Alfre and Alice and Cromwell. They joined our family effortlessly. Because we'd done seven TV seasons, 182 episodes, and a movie already together, we were thick as thieves and still are; may Patrick rest in peace. The three of them joined us as if we’d been dancing with them forever.".

#173637. More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations.
  • It has been revealed that A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a newly introduced explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries.
  • Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations. Scientists have debated the cause of this enormous gap for decades, but fresh research suggests that the answer may lie in the slow movement of entire continents, driven by powerful forces deep inside Earth.

It has been revealed that A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a newly introduced explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries. Published in the journal Nature, the findings suggest that ancient continents gradually rose and sank over hundreds of millions of years as hot rock moved through Earth's interior. These changes in elevation may have allowed erosion to remove enormous amounts of rock, erasing vast stretches of the planet's geological record.

Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.

Industry observers note that "Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance," he stated.

Earth's Mysterious Missing Billion Years.

In a recent development, normally, layers of sedimentary rock accumulate over time, creating a geological timeline in which older rocks lie beneath younger ones. Scientists can study these layers to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

Yet this timeline contains a remarkable interruption. At numerous locations worldwide, sedimentary rocks dating to the Cambrian period, around 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite that can be more than a billion years old. The intervening geological layers are absent, leaving an enormous break in the record known as the Great Unconformity.

One of the clearest examples is visible in the Grand Canyon in the United States. This region was once part of Laurentia (modern North America), an ancient continental landmass. Similar gaps have been identified in Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia.

In a recent development, the amount of missing time varies considerably between locations. In some places, approximately 200 million years of geological history are absent, while elsewhere the gap exceeds a billion years.

How Forces Deep Inside Earth May Have Erased the Rock Record.

To investigate what caused these missing chapters, Dhungana worked with his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, to simulate the movement of Earth's mantle over hundreds of millions of years.

In a recent development, the mantle is an immense layer of hot, mostly solid rock beneath Earth's crust. Although this material appears rigid on human timescales, it can deform and flow extremely slowly over geological periods. Heat-driven circulation within the mantle, a process called mantle convection, can gradually raise enormous regions of Earth's surface or cause them to subside.

These vertical movements can influence whether ancient rocks are exposed to erosion or buried beneath new deposits. When a continent rises, wind, water and other natural processes can gradually wear away its surface. If the land later sinks, oceans can advance over it, allowing fresh sediment to accumulate on top of the eroded rock.

The researchers found that this process may explain both the disappearance of ancient rock layers and the preservation of the geological boundary that remains visible today.

Ancient Continents Rose and Sank Over Millions of Years.

The simulations revealed a striking pattern across three major ancient continental regions: Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe) and North China.

According to recent reports, according to the models, mantle convection caused the ancient cores of these continents to rise during the Neoproterozoic Era, which extended from roughly one billion to 540 million years ago. This long interval preceded the Cambrian period, when animal life underwent a remarkable expansion in diversity, commonly known as the Cambrian explosion.

As the continents remained elevated, prolonged erosion could have stripped away extensive layers of older rock, gradually removing hundreds of millions of years of geological history.

The researchers found that this period of uplift was followed by widespread subsidence during the Phanerozoic eon, which encompasses approximately the past 540 million years. As these ancient continental regions slowly sank, advancing seas covered their eroded surfaces. Latest sediments accumulated above the exposed older rocks, preserving the boundary between the two.

Over immense spans of time, this sequence of uplift, erosion, subsidence and sediment deposition could have produced the Great Unconformity seen in rock formations today.

A Fresh Explanation for One of Earth's Greatest Geological Mysteries.

A particularly important finding was how closely the computer simulations matched the geographical distribution of the Great Unconformity.

The models predicted long-term uplift followed by subsidence in North America, northern Europe and North China, precisely the regions where the geological gap is especially well documented and preserved.

It has been revealed that this agreement provides support for the idea that deep mantle movements played a major role in shaping the missing rock record. Rather than requiring a separate explanation for each location, the findings suggest that a common process operating deep within Earth may account for the widespread pattern.

According to recent reports, "Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface," Associate Professor Flament said.

The research offers a way to connect the geological evidence visible at Earth's surface with the slow processes occurring far below it. Although the findings do not establish that mantle convection was the only factor responsible for the Great Unconformity, they provide a testable explanation for why so much ancient geological history disappeared and how the remaining evidence survived.

"Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle.".

Is Spotify still tracking your listening for Wrapped 2026? Heres what we know.

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that every year, as Spotify Wrapped season approaches, a familiar kind of panic sets in.
  • In a recent development, recently, someone asked me who I thought my top artist would be this year, and for the first time in a long time, I genuinely had no idea.
  • Industry observers note that after all, Spotify Wrapped isn't just a recap of what you listened to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that every year, as Spotify Wrapped season approaches, a familiar kind of panic sets in. You start mentally calculating how many times you've streamed your favorite artist, wondering whether that one song you played obsessively in Feb. will come back to haunt you, and perhaps making a last-minute attempt to influence your results.

In a recent development, recently, someone asked me who I thought my top artist would be this year, and for the first time in a long time, I genuinely had no idea. Stray Kids have held that spot for the past four years, but with fewer upcoming releases from the group in 2026, my listening habits have been a little more unpredictable. I've spent the year bouncing between artists and genres, which means my top five could be anyone's guess. (And yes, I'm a little nervous about that.).

Industry observers note that after all, Spotify Wrapped isn't just a recap of what you listened to. It's become a public declaration of your musical identity, one that inevitably ends up on Instagram Stories for everyone to judge.

It has been revealed that but with Nov. nearly over and Spotify Wrapped 2026 expected to arrive in early Dec., there's one vital question: Is Spotify still tracking your listening habits?

The answer is a little complicated.

Spotify has not confirmed the exact cutoff date for Wrapped 2026. However, based on how the tech giant has handled previous editions, your listening data likely stopped counting sometime in mid-Nov.

For years, a persistent rumor suggested that Spotify stopped collecting data for Wrapped on Oct. 31, leaving the final two months of the year out of your annual recap. But that's not quite how it works.

In 2025, Spotify confirmed that Wrapped included listening activity from Jan. 1 through mid-Nov., just a few weeks before its Dec. 3 release. The organization explained that it needs time to process listening data and prepare millions of personalized recaps ahead of launch.

So while Spotify continues recording your listening activity for its regular features and recommendations, that doesn't necessarily mean your late-Nov. streams will count toward Wrapped 2026.

Until Spotify confirms this year's tracking window, there's no way to know for certain.

If you're hoping to push a particular artist into your top five before Wrapped arrives, you may already be out of luck.

Even if Spotify is still counting streams, a few days of obsessive listening probably won't dramatically change the habits you've accumulated over the past 11 months.

Industry observers note that but there's an important distinction between how Spotify calculates your top songs and top artists. According to Spotify's explanation of its Wrapped methodology, your top songs are ranked by the number of times you've listened to them, with each play counting after more than 30 seconds. Your top artists, meanwhile, are determined using a weighted stream count that gives primary artists more credit than featured performers.

That means an artist whose entire discography you've been listening to all year could rank higher than someone responsible for your single most-played song.

In other words, your Wrapped results aren't necessarily as straightforward as counting how many times you've played your favorite track.

It has been revealed that maybe you're less concerned about getting your favorite artist to No. 1 and more worried about the songs you don't want showing up in your results. Fortunately, Spotify gives users some control over what influences their Wrapped.

Sources indicate that in a Nov. 5 announcement, Spotify reminded listeners that they can exclude individual tracks and playlists from their Taste Profile, preventing those streams from influencing certain Wrapped results and everyday recommendations.

Open Spotify and find the track or playlist.

Select "Exclude from your taste profile." (You can reverse the decision by selecting "Include in your taste profile.").

Spotify claims this setting applies to past and future listening, meaning you can remove a particularly embarrassing musical obsession from your taste-based results even after you've spent hours streaming it.

There's also a dedicated setting for kids' and family music, which is especially useful for parents who don't want their children's favorite songs dominating their year-end recap.

Industry observers note that one caveat: Excluded listening can still contribute to your total minutes listened. It just won't shape your taste-based rankings.

Spotify hasn't announced an official release date, but Wrapped typically arrives in late Nov. or early Dec.

Industry observers note that last year's edition launched on Dec. 3, while the 2024 and 2023 editions arrived on Dec. 4 and Nov. 29, respectively. If Spotify follows its recent pattern of Wednesday releases, Dec. 2, 2026, is a possibility, though the firm has yet to confirm that date.

According to recent reports, until then, you can keep listening to whatever you want. Whether those streams make it into your Wrapped is another question entirely.

It has been revealed that and perhaps that's for the best. The fun of Spotify Wrapped has always been discovering what your listening habits reveal about you, even when the results aren't quite what you expected.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Studio star admitted that he had a less than stellar time guest starring on Dawson’s Creek in 2003, adding he felt some tensions among the cast and crew.
  • According to recent reports, “I hated that,” Rogen confessed on the Nov.
  • The 44-year-old explained that he was convinced to appear on the season six episode “Rock Bottom” by his former Freaks and Geeks costar and Dawson’s Creek actress Busy Philipps after she appeared on his show Undeclared.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Seth Rogen couldn’t wait for this gig to be over.

The Studio star admitted that he had a less than stellar time guest starring on Dawson’s Creek in 2003, adding he felt some tensions among the cast and crew.

According to recent reports, “I hated that,” Rogen confessed on the Nov. 16 episode of the Happy Sad Confused podcast. “That was not fun.”.

The 44-year-old explained that he was convinced to appear on the season six episode “Rock Bottom” by his former Freaks and Geeks costar and Dawson’s Creek actress Busy Philipps after she appeared on his show Undeclared.

According to recent reports, “She was like, ‘Hey, now that I’m doing this, you gotta do Dawson’s Creek.’ And I was like, ‘Haha,’” Rogen recalled. “And then, like, six months later, I’m on the set of Dawson’s Creek. I was like, ‘How did this happen?’”.

And according to the Emmy winner, the drama wasn’t just onscreen, as he revealed there was plenty behind-the-scenes, too.

“It was so weird,” he shared. “And there was a lot of resentment between, like, the showrunners and the cast—it was a very bad dynamic.”.

He had quite a harrowing experience away from the set, too, adding, “I was staying in, like, a haunted hotel and had a nervous breakdown.”.

E! News has reached out to Dawson’s Creek creator Kevin Williamson, as well as showrunners Greg Berlanti and Tom Kapinos for comment but has not heard back.

Kapinos previously expressed his own frustration with the series that ran from 1998 to 2003 and starred the late James Van Der Beek, Katie Holmes, Joshua Jackson and Michelle Williams.

"The experience was miserable," he shared during a 2009 Emmys panel. "But it was a four-year boot camp. It was like going to TV grad school and learning how to run a television show. Anybody on that show who could make a decision was allowed to run it at some point. I inherited the very awkward college years, and I almost ran the show into the ground. But I learned everything that I needed to know about how to run a show.".

Still, he was far from the only resident of the Creek who had issues during the series, as Williams explained being on the show for so long deterred her from doing television for a number of years as she feared a “loss of input.”.

As Williams explained, being on the show for so long deterred her from doing television for a number of years as she feared a “loss of input.”.

In a recent development, “Doing Dawson’s Creek for six-and-a-half years, while it was an incredible learning experience—we did 22 episodes a year, and you’d be getting scripts at the last minute and you had zero input,” she shared with actress Patricia Clarkson during an interview for Variety in 2019. “It was a little like a factory job. It was formulaic.”.

For more secrets from the set of Dawson’s Creek, keep reading.

While Fox was first to pick up Dawson's Creek, it subsequently dumped the teen drama.

"I was told they were struggling with Party of Five and they didn't need another one," series creator Kevin Williamson said at the 2015 ATX TV Festival.

But that paved the way for The WB to pick it up two years later.

While Paula Cole's "I Don't Want to Wait" became the iconic Dawson's Creek theme song, producers originally wanted Alanis Morissette's "Hand in My Pocket.".

Alas, they couldn't land the rights, what a jagged little pill.

Dawson. Pacey. Joey. Not names you hear every day. So how did Williamson come up with them?

"Dawson came from a real place called Dawson's Creek where we all hung out as kids and partied," he told The Hollywood Reporter in 2018, while Pacey "came from a friend of a friend named Pacey and I'd never met anyone with that name and thought it was a cool name.".

And for the show's heroine, Williamson "wanted Josephine as a very girly name that could easily turn into a tomboy name like Joey.".

Remember Dawson's infamous "walk the dog" line in the pilot?

Williamson inserted the euphemism because the network would not let them say the word "masturbate" in 1998.

Before Katie Holmes was cast in the role that would make her America's sweetheart-next-door, Blair was this close to landing the role.

Sources indicate that "Joe was written to be a tomboy and everyone was coming in being very much a tomboy. We were very close to going with Selma Blair, who was amazing," Williamson told THR. "She read it very tough, with a lot of heart.".

However, once he saw Holmes on tape, with "those two big eyes," Williamson knew they had their Joey.

Joshua Jackson Was Almost Dawson.

Williamson liked Joshua Jackson so much, he didn't care what role the Mighty Ducks alum played.

"I fell in love with Josh Jackson because he could read any role, Dawson or Pacey," he told THR. "But something wasn't complete and that's when the network said they didn't see Josh as Dawson, and rightfully so. So, I went, 'OK, he's Pacey,' because I knew I wanted him in the show no matter what.".

Charlie Hunnam Auditioned, Won Role of Husband.

An 18-year-old Charlie Hunnam read for the WB drama in 1999 and, while he didn't land the part, he did meet Katherine Towne at his audition.

They tied the knot in Las Vegas three weeks later and divorced in 2002, "three terrible, painful, expensive years later," as Hunnam put it to the Associated Press in 2017.

Dawson's Creek became so popular that American Eagle inked a deal in 2000 to outfit the actors.

The characters wore mostly AE clothes throughout season three, and the cast appeared in ad campaigns and promos for the clothing line, helping drive the organization's net income above $105 million in 2001.

When James Van Der Beek was first cast, the studio wanted him to change his hair.

In a recent development, "We found an ad for The Devil's Own, the movie with Brad Pitt," he recalled to The Daily Beast in 2012. "They said: 'What about Brad Pitt's haircut?' That's how I got my season one haircut.".

Joey and Pacey's Real-Life Love.

Holmes dated Jackson early in the show's run, before Pacey and Joey realized they opposite-of-hated each other.

It has been revealed that "I'm just going to say that I met somebody last year," Holmes told Rolling Stone in 1998, not denying that the somebody was Jackson. "I fell in love, I had my first love, and it was something so incredible and indescribable that I will treasure it always. And that I feel so fortunate because he's now one of my best friends. It's weird, it's almost like a Dawson-and-Joey type thing now.".

Plus one more nugget: "He's been in the business so long," she added, "and he's really helped me. I respect him as a friend and a professional.".

Kerr Smith Didn't Know Jack Was Gay.

When Kerr Smith first signed on to join the show as Joey's fresh boyfriend, he had no idea the character would eventually come out and be part of the first-ever gay kiss on TV.

In a recent development, "I always knew I wanted Jack to come out of the closet, but I didn't even tell [Smith]," Williamson said at the ATX TV Festival. "Let the audience love him, then let's have him come out of the closet and have Joey have to deal with that—and then that would eventually drive her back to [Dawson].".

More poignantly, Williamson has said that every character on the show inherited traits from him, including Jack.

“Every single character has a trait of me in them,” he told Entertainment Weekly in 2018. “I had just, in my 20s, gone through the coming-out process and had told my parents I was gay. I had taken that whole journey, and I wanted a character on the show to represent that journey and to represent that side of me.".

Jack's coming out episode, cowritten by Williamson and producer Greg Berlanti, was inspired by true events.

"A friend of mine had a story that I brought in that he got outed accidentally," Berlanti told EW, "because he wrote a love poem that it was so clear to everyone else that it was about a guy.”.

Michelle Williams and Busy Philipps' best-friendship, which first blossomed on Dawson's Creek, is still going strong to this day.

“I’m so in love with her,” Williams told People of her bestie at a 2016 screening of Manchester by the Sea, one of many red carpet date nights for the besties. “She’s proof that the love of your life does not have to be a man! That’s the love of my life right there.”.

Philipps is also godmother to Williams' daughter Matilda Ledger, who was born in 2005.

Dawson finally losing his virginity was such a big show moment that Van Der Beek brought a very special gift to set the day the scene was filmed.

"I remember bringing champagne for the crew—Dawson finally lost his virginity!" he told The Daily Beast.

Chad Michael Murray, One Tree Heel?

Before starring on One Tree Hill, Chad Michael Murray had an arc on Dawson's Creek playing Charlie, a love interest for Jen and Joey.

But while Charlie got around, Murray didn't seem to make a lot of friends during his first stint in North Carolinav (OTH later filmed there).

Sources indicate that during a Paley panel in 2009, Philipps called him "a douche," later saying, "Don't worry. I'm not real worried about burning bridges with CMM.".

Van Der Beek added, "He's actually come a long way." Post-event, Philipps tweeted, "Just finished the dawson's creek panel. Maybe I was too harsh on chadM2… Nah.".

Murray, meanwhile, hasn't stirred the pot, saying in 2015 that he learned a lot from the experience.

“I had the opportunity to learn from people who had been doing it for a couple of years longer than I was when I walked into the Dawson’s cast,” he told Cosmpolitan.com in 2015. “You know, Michelle and James and Katie and Josh—they really kind of guided me, because they’d already been around for five, six years, maybe longer. And if they had the time, they were showing me the ropes. I had no idea what lighting was, I had no idea about a lot of the technical aspects of what we do, and so I’m grateful for that experience.”.

Just a sampling of the famous faces, ranging from the already familiar to future huge stars, who appeared on Dawson's Creek over the years: Seth Rogen, Jane Lynch, Julie Bowen, Scott Foley, Jensen Ackles, Hilarie Burton, Rachel Leigh Cook, Ali Larter and Oliver Hudson.

Young Americans was a short-lived spinoff centering on Pacey's friend Will Krudski (Rodney Scott) and his boarding school classmates at Rawley Academy.

Also starring Ian Somerhalder and Kate Bosworth, it was canceled after just one season.

The Show Almost Ended With Joey Picking Dawson.

The show's main love triangle officially disassembled when Joey chose Pacey in the 2003 series finale.

But it almost didn't turn out that way, as Williamson first envisioned Dawson getting the girl. But halfway through writing the finale, Williamson realized that a happy ending for that couple wasn't "what the show was set to be.".

It has been revealed that "I wanted it to be a twist on the teen genre but also wanted it to be surprising, honest and real and say something about soul mates and what soul mates can be," he explained at the ATX TV Festival. "That's why we did it that way. When you left the show in that last moment, they're a family and everyone got what they wanted. There was fulfillment and they were all happy.".

At the last minute, he changed his mind and the rest is TV history. But Williamson admitted his mom, who played for Team Dawson, was not happy.

In the finale, which jumped ahead five years, the group had to deal with the devastating loss of Jen.

"Dealing with the death of one of their own was the final thing that thrust them into adulthood forever. Dawson's Creek was a coming-of-age story and that was the idea behind that ending," Williamson explained of the decision. "That's why we killed Jen, because I wanted them to deal with a death of one their own as that final lesson.".

Some of the executive producers who get their start on Dawson's?

Julie Plec (who went on to gift us with The Vampire Diaries and The Originals), Berlanti (Everwood, Arrow, The Flash, Riverdale...the list goes on and on, and that doesn't even include his movies), Rob Thomas (Veronica Mars and iZombie), Jenny Bicks (Sex and the City), Anna Fricke (Being Human), Dana Baratta (Jessica Jones) and many more.

The Feds Left Iowans in the Dark About Aims to Blow Up Tons of Lead

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1143 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On October 26, Charles Massner, the mayor of Mediapolis, Iowa, got an email from the US Army.
  • In a recent development, the email, which was reviewed by WIRED, provided no details about when this explosion would happen, how much material the explosion would destroy, or what steps officials should take to protect the public from a possible toxic fallout.
  • Recent findings suggest that massner says the next time he heard anything was early last week, when the Army published a press release on its website saying it would explode the lead azide in just a few days.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On October 26, Charles Massner, the mayor of Mediapolis, Iowa, got an email from the US Army. It described “an intentional, controlled detonation” of “a quantity of degraded lead azide … in the near future” at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, some 20 miles south of Mediapolis.

In a recent development, the email, which was reviewed by WIRED, provided no details about when this explosion would happen, how much material the explosion would destroy, or what steps officials should take to protect the public from a possible toxic fallout. But it did request that public officials allow for environmental testing on public lands before and after the event, which the town granted in a November 2 meeting.

Recent findings suggest that massner says the next time he heard anything was early last week, when the Army published a press release on its website saying it would explode the lead azide in just a few days. That press release included a map of potential exposure from the blast. Mediapolis was directly in the path of exposure, covered in a reddish-yellow cloud with a hot pink border.

“There was really no communication, so to speak, other than what was on their website,” he states.

Massner wasn’t alone in being caught off guard. The sudden announcement that the Army would be exploding 9,500 pounds of lead azide with seemingly little to no notice caught nearly all of Iowa by surprise. Governor Kim Reynolds’ office said last week that they’d learned about the explosion the same way Massner did: via the press release sent out by the Army on November 15.

In a recent development, now, despite a court order blocking the detonation, the Army announced late Sunday night that it intends to blow up the lead azide on Wednesday, a day before the Thanksgiving holiday. (On Monday, President Donald Trump posted that he was ordering the Army not to detonate anything without court approval.) Many Iowans are left with more questions than answers. Iowa’s unofficial state subreddit is filled with posts from people trying to strategy holiday travel and safety around the event, which has switched dates twice in the past week. One local official in the path of a potential fallout told WIRED on Friday that she was leaving the area and staying at a hotel with her immunocompromised child.

Peter Thorne, a professor of environmental health at the University of Iowa who has studied exposure to lead in his laboratory, claims his lab has been “deluged with concerns,” with everyone from pediatricians to parents to people who run cleaning facilities and are worried about their staff exposure reaching out. Like most Iowans, Thorne also heard about the explosion from the Army’s press release.

“My first reaction was, They’re going to do what?” he notes.

The 68 barrels of degraded lead azide at the Middletown site have been there for more than 20 years. In March, according to a document released by the Army on November 18, the material was officially labeled hazardous waste, and officials began looking into how to dispose of it. In a court filing published Saturday, the Army says that there is an “immediate risk” of the material exploding by itself after temperatures drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit. It is now invoking emergency powers to detonate the barrels by November 24.

“In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion,” the filing states.

The Army did not immediately respond to a list of questions sent by WIRED.

Sources indicate that the Army does seem to have looked into other options besides blowing up the azide. The New York Times reported Friday that the Army awarded a contract in late March to a private company to handle cleaning up the chemicals onsite. However, that contract was pulled two months later; the company told the Times that the Army did not give a reason for changing its mind on the cleanup. A contracting officer in the Army told the company that the Army’s decision to pursue detonation “was not based on deficiencies” with the company’s science.

In a letter sent to Governor Reynolds on Friday, the EPA Region 7 administrator noted that the agency only learned that the material had degraded to a dangerous state in March. The letter also listed a number of strategies the EPA had considered besides detonation, including chemical cleanup, which also risked causing an explosion.

Sources indicate that the Army has blown up expired munitions before, although not at the scale of what it plans to do in Iowa. Thorne states that any exposure to lead from the explosion is expected to be “quite a bit lower” than lead exposures in communities exposed to legacy pollution sources. But “there is no safe level for lead, especially for young children,” he says.

The Army did have some public meetings and communications in late October with officials in Middletown, where the explosion will take place and where it has recommended temporary evacuation measures for some neighborhoods. But it’s not clear why its initial direct outreach around public health didn’t extend to towns in potential fallout ranges for a blast, including Mediapolis, beyond asking for permission to test soil samples. (The Army did include recommended public health measures in its November 15 press release.).

Thorne, a former chair of the EPA’s Science Advisory Board, says that a successful public health outreach program has lots of opportunity for public engagement for all affected areas.

“You have public meetings. You answer questions. You have extensive Q&A and FAQs, and you have people speaking to why this is the only choice, what are the burdens, and some kind of a cost-benefit comparison between the options, and then you roll it out through the media, through social media, through many ways,” he states. “Best practice is not what they’ve done—I think this is closer to worst practice, from a public health perspective.”.

Industry observers note that for his part, Massner, Mediapolis’s mayor, mentioned on Friday that he planned to take “standard precautions” and follow the Army’s public health recommendations. (The Army has not released fallout modeling for a Wednesday explosion, but if winds carry the material south, it would be possible for Mediapolis to no longer be in the affected zone.) But Massner says he understands why people in his town were freaked out.

Industry observers note that “What people saw was the map they drew, which indicated a [red] cloud going over everybody’s head. I don’t think that was the intent of the map,” he laughs. “When you see a map covered in red, you’re supposed to run for shelter immediately—your life is in danger.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this Wednesday (Nov. 25) marks 20 years since the assassination of Valentín Elizalde, the regional Mexican singer who, at the height of his career, was gunned down after a performance in Reynosa, in northern Mexico, along with his manager Mario Mendoza and his driver Reynaldo Ballesteros. To this day, the reasons or culprits behind the crime remain unknown.

In a recent development, at just 27 years old, the singer from Sonora was already an icon, thanks to his commanding personality and unique interpretive style, accompanied by Sinaloan banda music. Despite not possessing a powerful voice, Elizalde poured emotion into songs like “Vete Ya,” “Cómo Me Duele,” “Vencedor” and “Te Quiero Así,” which have become timeless classics in Mexican music.

During his lifetime, “El Gallo de Oro” (The Golden Rooster), as he was known, entered the top 10 of Billboard‘s Regional Mexican Airplay chart in 2003 with his hit “Vete Ya.” After his death, his album Vencedor, which had been released months earlier, reached No. 1 on both Top Latin Albums and Top Regional Mexican Albums. His posthumous set Lobo Domesticado, released in January 2007, peaked at No. 2 on Top Latin Albums and was nominated for a Latin Grammy for best banda album. In 2009, he competed in the same category with the compilation Solamente El Gallo de Oro.

According to recent reports, elizalde’s legacy has transcended time, with newly introduced generations of regional Mexican artists paying homage to him in their concerts and through new versions of his hits. For example, Edgardo Nuñez recorded two tribute albums in his honor this year.

Below, find 10 songs from “El Gallo de Oro” that are essential for any playlist to remember him today, two decades after his passing.

It has been revealed that from the album Mi Satisfacción (2003), “Vete Ya” is the most-streamed song by Valentín Elizalde on digital platforms. This heartbreak anthem speaks about the decision to walk away from a meaningless relationship when love no longer exists. “Leave already/ If you can’t find reasons to stay with me/ Why continue?”), he states firmly about what cannot be saved.

Undoubtedly the most musically cheerful track and one of Elizalde’s classics. The simple, uncomplicated lyrics speak about jealousy and the pain of others getting close to the loved one. The chorus, which is repeated many times, states it all: “Oh, how it hurts me when they ask you for a dance.” Written by Manuel Rodríguez Figueroa, it is part of the 2006 album Vencedor.

It has been revealed that A great admirer of Joan Sebastian, Elizalde recorded his version of the hit song “Lobo Domesticado” nearly ten years after its original release, giving it a unique twist with his distinctive style. The song is part of his 2005 album of the same name, released during the height of his career.

According to recent reports, the song corresponds to the early success of Valentín Elizalde and remains one of his most streamed tracks on digital platforms. “Ebrio de Amor,” written by Humberto González, is part of the album Traición Federal (2000), and speaks of a profound love, with verses like: “I arrived drunk with love/ Like every night/ You will want to kiss me and fill me with love/ Without any reproach.”.

According to recent reports, “Vencedor” is the title of the song and album released on April 18, 2006, which catapulted the rising career of Elizalde. No one could have imagined that seven months later, this production would be the one to take him to the top of the charts as a reaction to his death. Written by Benny Camacho, it speaks of an unconditional love that overcomes any obstacle.

In 1987, José José turned Rafael Pérez Botija’s song “Soy Así” into a classic of romantic ballads. Eighteen years later, Valentín Elizalde gave it a upcoming twist with his voice and, accompanied by a Sinaloan banda, made it an essential hit in regional Mexican music. The song, which gave its name to the album it was included in, perfectly described “The Golden Rooster”: “I’m like this/ This is how I was born and this is how I’ll die/ With all my flaws, I know.”.

Another gem from the album Vencedor, this song — whose title means “To My Enemies” — sparked controversy as it was thought to have been written for a figure in the world of drug trafficking. However, the songwriter Alejandro Lira recently clarified in the HBO Max docuseries The Killing of the Golden Rooster that it was not commissioned. “No one gave me anything/ Everything I have is mine/ With the sweat of my brow/ I have achieved what I wanted,” claims the song with a strong and direct message.

With a rhythmic cadence, this song talks about a woman who is not happy with the way she is, and her partner helps her see that she is beautiful and doesn’t need to change anything to be loved. Performed by Elizalde, the message carried even more emotion for the fans who made it one of their favorites.

The most romantic song by the singer from Sonora is also one that cannot be missing from a Valentín Elizalde playlist. Included in the 2004 album Volveré A Amar, it talks about an idealized woman, the one who keeps him up at night and for whom he would give everything: “Nothing compares to you/ No one compares to you/ You are someone special/ You are my best reason.”.

In a recent development, cumbia and joy have always been a part of Elizalde’s discography, and “La Playa” is one of his danceable tracks that has remained timeless. The song, written by José Luis Cornejo, talks about the unexpected encounter of a man on a beach with a woman who captivates him with her gaze and her movements. It is part of the album Regresan Los Mafiosos, released in 2005.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability concerns and to inspire positive action.

In a recent development, originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Massive Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo. Nowadays, it is more loosely used to refer to some of Africa’s largest and most iconic animals.

It has been revealed that however, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “New Big Five” for wildlife photography. In 2021, 50,000 people around the world voted for the five animals they would most like to photograph, or see photographed, in the wild. Five animals were crowned the winners: the elephant, polar bear, lion, gorilla and tiger.

This week, sees the publication of “The New Big 5” photography book, which features images of those animals and other at-risk wildlife, from photography legends such as Ami Vitale, Steve McCurry and Paul Nicklen, and essays from famous conservationists and activists including like Jane Goodall and Paula Kahumbu.

Green indicates that the book celebrates wildlife and is a global call to action on complications impacting wildlife, including habitat loss, poaching, pollution and climate change.

Green was on assignment in Botswana at least a decade ago when he came up with the idea for a project to encourage people to “shoot with a camera, not a gun,” he states.

“I thought this would be a way to get people really focusing on wildlife, thinking about the wildlife they love, thinking about the animals that are at risk.”.

Ten photographs that made the world wake up to climate change.

In total, the book includes the work of 144 globally renowned wildlife photographers from Ecuador to India. Curating the images took nearly two years of work, indicates Green.

“I think these are some of the most beautiful and creative images that I’ve seen put together in one book,” says Green. “These are the species that we are at risk of losing.”.

In a recent development, according to the UN, nature is declining at an unprecedented rate, with around one million of the planet’s animal and plant species facing extinction. The “Fresh Massive 5,” all of which are threatened, act as ambassadors for what is happening in the natural world, says Green.

As well as being a powerful reminder of what we stand to lose, the book also points people towards potential solutions. Featured essays explore the benefits of rewilding and the importance of indigenous communities in conservation.

A chapter on endangered species from bees to blue whales illustrates the alarming threat climate change poses to animals outside of the “New Significant 5.” “That’s only the tip of the iceberg – I could have included thousands of pictures because that’s how serious the situation is,” says Green.

Why a wildlife photographer took 40,000 photos to capture these extraordinary birds.

Jane Goodall, a leading conservationist who also wrote the afterword to the book, noted in a press release that “we have a window of time during which we can start to heal some of the harm we have inflicted on the natural world, but only if we get together and take action now.

Sources indicate that “I hope the photos will lead people into the wonderful worlds of these iconic species. Then, perhaps, other people will become involved in helping to create a world where wildlife can flourish for future generations to enjoy,” she remarked.

“The Fresh Big 5: A Global Photography Project For Endangered Wildlife,” by Graeme Green, published by Earth Aware Editions, is on sale from April 4, 2023.

This story has been updated to reflect the range of concerns covered by the book.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn. Scientists have eliminated several suspected sources of the ancient sandstone slab, narrowing the search for where it originated thousands of years ago.

A fresh study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.

Measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England. For more than a century, archaeologists and geologists believed it had been transported from Wales. However, recent research using advanced analytical methods overturned that long-standing theory and identified northeastern Scotland as a more likely source.

Now, a new international investigation has refined the search even further, although the stone's exact birthplace remains unknown.

Latest Geological Clues Narrow the Search.

To investigate the Altar Stone's origins, researchers combined fresh observations of the monument with detailed examinations of stone fragments preserved in museum collections.

Sources indicate that using multiple scientific techniques, the team studied the sandstone's physical structure, mineral content, chemical composition, and isotopic signatures. Together, these characteristics provide a distinctive geological fingerprint that can be compared with rock formations across Britain.

The scientists focused particular attention on the Orcadian Basin in northeastern Scotland, an area previously identified as a promising candidate. However, none of the locations examined so far has produced rock with the same combination of characteristics as the Altar Stone.

Although the findings have not revealed the stone's original location, they allow researchers to eliminate several possibilities and concentrate future investigations on more promising areas.

Professor Duncan Pirrie, Emeritus Professor at the University of South Wales and leader of the study, explained:.

Recent findings suggest that "This is the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken. By combining a wide range of analytical techniques, we have built the clearest picture yet of the stone's composition and tested the leading theories about its origins. So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone. That tells us the search is not over, but we are now far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer.".

From Wales to Scotland: A Century-Old Theory Overturned.

For generations, the prevailing explanation placed the Altar Stone's origins in western Wales. That assumption changed when earlier scientific investigations revealed evidence pointing much farther north, toward Scotland.

The latest findings build on that discovery by establishing more precise geological criteria for identifying a potential match.

Professor Richard Bevins, Honorary Professor in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, noted:.

In a recent development, "For almost a century, the prevailing view was that the Altar Stone came from west Wales. Our previous research overturned that assumption and pointed instead to Scotland as the most likely source. This latest study significantly refines the search by identifying the specific geological characteristics we need to look for, allowing future investigations to be targeted more effectively. With each new piece of evidence, we move closer to solving one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.".

Rather than disproving Scotland as a possible source, the fresh investigation helps scientists distinguish between rock formations that appear promising and those that do not match the stone's distinctive properties.

Solving Stonehenge's Six-Ton Mystery.

Industry observers note that determining where the Altar Stone came from could reveal much more than the birthplace of a single rock. It could also help explain how prehistoric communities acquired and transported enormous stones over remarkable distances.

Stonehenge was constructed in multiple stages between approximately 3000 and 1600 BC. Its builders are known to have moved massive stones across the landscape, including the smaller bluestones, which traveled roughly 225 kilometers (140 miles) from western Wales.

According to recent reports, if the Altar Stone originated in northeastern Scotland, its journey to Salisbury Plain would have been considerably longer. Establishing its precise source could therefore offer important clues about the transportation methods, organization, and engineering abilities of the people who built Stonehenge.

Professor Nick Pearce, Emeritus Professor of Geochemistry in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, emphasized why eliminating possible sources represents genuine progress:.

In a recent development, "In a geological detective story such as this, ruling out potential source areas is just as important as identifying upcoming ones. Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated. The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago.".

In a recent development, the researchers believe the detailed geological fingerprint developed during this investigation will guide future searches and could eventually identify the Altar Stone's original location. Such a discovery would help illuminate one of prehistoric Britain's most extraordinary engineering accomplishments.

The international research team included geologists and archaeologists from the United Kingdom, Canada, Italy, and Sweden. Participating organizations included the University of South Wales, Aberystwyth University, University College London, the University of Aberdeen, the University of Plymouth, the James Hutton Institute, the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, the University of Milano-Bicocca, and several industry partners.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brad Pitt is sitting out of this one adventure.

One week after attending the Los Angeles premiere of The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth in Los Angeles, the actor unexpectedly skipped the Netflix movie’s red carpet rollout in London due to illness.

Sources indicate that ahead of the Nov. 23 event, its organizers told British outlet The Independent in a statement that Pitt was “is no longer able to attend the premiere as he has come down with flu and has been advised not to travel.".

Amid his sickness, the 62-year-old made the decision to focus on the long-term health of himself and his cast.

In a recent development, “He has had the flu for a few days and didn’t want to get anyone sick,” a source close to Pitt told E! News. “He is recovering and looking forward to future screenings.”.

Pitt’s costars Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and Peter Weller, as well as director David Fincher, still attended the premiere, which was held at the BFI IMAX in the English capital.

While Pitt may not have been present at The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’s latest premiere, the film—a sequel to Quentin Tarantino’s 2019 movie Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood—is missing his onscreen wingman Leonardo DiCaprio entirely after the Titanic alum opted to sit out.

"It would have been great fun, but it required a lot of prosthetics, which is a good couple of weeks prepping to get him," Pitt told The Hollywood Reporter earlier this month, referring to how the trailer teased that DiCaprio's Rick Dalton character had become "too fat" for his titular stuntman to serve as a body double. "It’s hardly worth the cost for a cameo.".

He added, "It was talked about for a while, but it just seemed like a big ask.”.

And DiCaprio confirmed he wouldn’t reprise his role ahead of the sequel, too.

Industry observers note that “There were some talks about it early on,” he told Deadline last year. Still, he added, “Ultimately, I cannot wait to see the Cliff Booth story, but I’m not in it.”.

While Pitt is returning to reprise his Oscar-winning role, read on to learn about the legendary parts he turned down.

Pitt was almost the One. "I did pass on 'The Matrix," the superstar recently admitted at the Santa Barbara International Film Festival in January. "I took the red pill. That's the only one I'm naming…I wasn't offered two or three. Only the first one, just to clarify that.".

As we all know, Keanu Reeves went on to be Neo, and is currently filming the fourth film in the franchise, though producer Lorenzeo di Bonaventura once revealed Will Smith, Leonardo DiCaprio and Sandra Bullock were all in consideration in addition to Pitt.

While it's hard to imagine anyone but Billy Crudup as Russell Hammond in Cameron Crowe's 2000 classic Almost Famous, Pitt was originally set to play the complicated rocker. But, according to the writer and director, who wrote the part with the star in mind, Pitt worked with Crowe for months before ultimately leaving the project, making way for Crudup to have his breakthrough performance.

"His head was still in Fight Club and the part was a little underwritten. It was the most underwritten in the script, and he couldn't trust it enough," Crowe told AL.com in 2014. "I've talked to him since. I love the guy. I think he's hilarious, and I thought he would have been funny in the movie. If I had waited a few more months, he might have come around to it, but we had to get going. But Billy Crudup worked out great.".

In a recent development, while it's widely considered one of the best films of all-time, Pitt infamously pulled out of the movie, with Gil Bellows ultimately taking over the small but pivotal role of prisoner Tommy. "These are the adventures in castings," director Frank Darabont told USA Today. "But it would be really fun to bump into Brad Pitt and say, 'Weren't you that guy?' I'd love to give him a little (grief) about that just for fun.".

After just landing his breakout role in Thelma & Louise, he ultimately decided to star in Interview With the Vampire over Shawshank. And he told the publication he had no regrets. "It would have been kind of cool to be in, but I'm not a regret guy in that way," he explained. "I just believe in the way things work out, and that was someone else's role. Even the feeling of, 'Ooh, that would've been nice' would redirect a choice later down the road. So it all works in tandem in that way.".

After working together on Ocean's 11, Matt Damon ended up snagging the lead role as spy Jason Bourne in The Bourne Identity when Pitt became unavailable, ironically, due to his commitment to Spy Game. After he reportedly passed, Damon received the offer that would result in a major movie franchise that has grossed over $1.6 billion worldwide.

In a recent development, did you know Pitt and Leonardo DiCaprio almost worked together years before finally collaborating on Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood? Pitt had originally bought the rights to remake the Hong Kong hit Internal Affairs, which ultimately became The Departed, with him slated to play Sullivan. But when the star dropped out, saying a younger actor should play the part—"I thought I was too old for it," he told Interview—Matt Damon once again filled in, with Pitt remaining a producer on the film.

While Christian Bale ultimately took on the murderous role of Patrick Batemen, turning in one of his most memorable performances, an earlier version of the film was set to star Pitt and be directed by David Cronenberg before creative differences halted the project.

"Yes, in the early Nineties with a young actor attached named Brad Pitt. David was lovely—is lovely, I still like David—but he had strange demands. He hated shooting restaurant scenes, and he hated shooting nightclub scenes," writer Bret Easton Ellis revealed to Rolling Stone. "And he didn't want to shoot the violence. I ignored everything he said. So of course he was disappointed with it and he hired his own writer; that script was worse for him and he dropped out.".

While he never technically auditioned for the part, there is a tape out there of Pitt reading the iconic role of J.D., which ultimately went to Christian Slater, at a table-read of Heathers ahead of its 1988 release.

"We just gathered actors that we knew and friends that we had to read the roles. And an actress named Stacey Travis—who was a friend of ours—was in an acting class and we didn't have anybody to read the part of J.D," director Michael Lehmann explained to Fandom. "So we asked Stacey and she brought this young kid from her class. A good looking kid, he cold-read part of J.D. in the table-read, and years later I found out if was Brad Pitt.".

Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1090 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A rare encounter nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface gave scientists an extraordinary opportunity to film one of the deep sea's most unusual creatures.
  • The discovery occurred during an expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard.
  • Members of MBARI's Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were investigating marine life approximately 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore when they spotted the fish about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A rare encounter nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface gave scientists an extraordinary opportunity to film one of the deep sea's most unusual creatures. Researchers from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) spotted a barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma), a mysterious species known for its transparent head and remarkable eyes that can rotate to track prey.

The discovery occurred during an expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard. It marked only the eleventh time MBARI scientists have encountered this elusive fish during nearly four decades of ocean exploration.

Members of MBARI's Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were investigating marine life approximately 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore when they spotted the fish about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface. Using the remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Doc Ricketts, the researchers were filming and collecting deep-sea organisms when the unexpected visitor appeared.

Industry observers note that "Seeing a barreleye fish is a rare treat. Crew from across the ship joined the science team in the control room, mesmerized by this remarkable animal. Deep-sea animals capture the imagination, creating wonder and awe that we hope will inspire stewardship of the largest living space on Earth," mentioned Senior Scientist Steven Haddock.

[See video link after end of article.].

A Surprise Encounter Deep in the Pacific Ocean.

Industry observers note that the discovery was an unexpected highlight of the eight-day Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition. Haddock and his colleagues had primarily been investigating gelatinous marine animals, including jellyfish, siphonophores, and ctenophores, also known as comb jellies. Their research seeks to understand how these delicate organisms have evolved to survive in the open ocean at great depths.

To investigate life throughout the water column, the team combined blue-water scuba dives near the surface with remotely operated vehicle surveys hundreds of meters below. These complementary approaches allowed researchers to observe and collect animals living in very different parts of the ocean.

Industry observers note that the barreleye appeared just as the day's underwater operations were coming to an end. The ROV pilots were "flying" Doc Ricketts toward the surface for recovery when Research Specialist Shannon Johnson noticed the unusual fish and immediately asked them to stop.

In a recent development, most of the scientists had already moved to the ship's wet lab, where they were preparing to catalog specimens collected during the dive. When word spread about the sighting, they hurried back to the control room, accompanied by crew members eager to see the extraordinary animal. The rare encounter provided an exciting conclusion to a busy and productive week of exploration.

How the Barreleye Fish Uses Its Transparent Head to Hunt.

Recent findings suggest that the barreleye's strange appearance is more than a biological curiosity. Its unusual anatomy helps it find food in the ocean's twilight zone, a dimly lit region where sunlight is faint and spotting prey can be difficult.

Earlier observations by MBARI Senior Scientist Bruce Robison and Research Specialist Kim Reisenbichler helped scientists understand how this remarkable fish hunts.

Sources indicate that rather than constantly swimming in search of food, Macropinna can remain nearly motionless in the water, supported by its large fins, which provide both stability and precise control over its movements. Its tubular eyes normally point upward, allowing it to watch for the faint silhouettes of animals passing overhead.

Recent findings suggest that once the fish detects something worth eating, its eyes can rotate within a transparent dome of tissue covering the top of its head. This unusual ability allows the barreleye to maintain visual contact with prey as it changes position to capture it.

Sources indicate that the clear, gelatinous covering serves another important purpose. Barreleyes can feed on small crustaceans trapped among the stinging tentacles of deep-sea siphonophores, which are colonial animals related to jellyfish. The protective dome helps shield the fish's sensitive eyes while it retrieves its meal.

Rare 4K Footage Reveals Extraordinary Details.

In a recent development, scientists were able to spend approximately 20 minutes watching the barreleye during the encounter. Using the high-resolution 4K camera aboard Doc Ricketts, they recorded unusually detailed views of its anatomy and movements.

The team also adjusted the vehicle's lighting to make the fish's transparent head shield easier to observe. These changes helped reveal the unusual structures that make this species so distinctive.

ROV Pilot/Technician Cameron Law brought Doc Ricketts close enough to capture additional footage with the vehicle's virtual reality camera. The resulting 3D stereo imagery provides another perspective on the fish and could eventually be used in educational programs and public outreach.

Sources indicate that "Macropinna reminds us of the surprising ways that animals have adapted to thrive in the ocean's midwater," mentioned Haddock. "So many of them survive by looking for subtle optical cues, like a shadow passing overhead, and this sets off evolutionary competition, pitting bioluminescent camouflage against increasingly sophisticated visual capabilities.".

An Extraordinary Sighting After Nearly 7,000 Deep-Sea Dives.

According to recent reports, the rarity of the encounter becomes even more striking when considering MBARI's extensive exploration history. Over nearly 40 years, the institute has conducted approximately 7,000 remotely operated vehicle dives and accumulated more than 41,000 hours of deep-sea video. Despite that enormous effort, researchers have recorded just 11 encounters with Macropinna microstoma.

Recent findings suggest that MBARI's previous sighting of Macropinna occurred in 2021. The latest encounter represents two important firsts for the institute: its first 4K footage of this species and its first observation of the fish from the upcoming flagship research vessel David Packard.

In a recent development, MBARI scientists have also encountered other members of the barreleye family during their ocean expeditions. This summer, researchers working with Schmidt Ocean Institute in the mid-Atlantic Ocean recorded another unusual deep-sea species, the binocular fish (Winteria telescopa).

Together, these encounters provide rare opportunities to observe the remarkable adaptations that allow animals to survive far beneath the ocean's surface, where light is scarce and much of the marine environment remains unexplored.

The Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition was supported through the David and Lucile Packard Foundation's longstanding commitment to MBARI's scientific research.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just days ago, Jensen Huang’s chances of returning as Nvidia CEO looked increasingly slim, at least according to prediction markets.
  • The swings in Huang’s odds on prediction markets offer a window into how his unlikely comeback unfolded and who saw it coming.
  • It has been revealed that on Sunday evening in Washington, Huang’s odds on Polymarket US jumped 6 percentage points in just 40 minutes after Trump published a Truth Social missive calling for Huang’s reinstatement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just days ago, Jensen Huang’s chances of returning as Nvidia CEO looked increasingly slim, at least according to prediction markets. Earlier this month, Huang resigned from the AI hardware giant following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence services. As more reports emerged about Huang’s alleged bad behavior, Nvidia’s board insisted it had no aims to reinstate him. By early Sunday morning on the East Coast, traders on Polymarket’s US platform put his chances of returning at just 10 percent. But by Monday, Huang was back in charge.

The swings in Huang’s odds on prediction markets offer a window into how his unlikely comeback unfolded and who saw it coming. The New York Times reported that President Trump played a crucial role in convincing the board to bring Huang back. Traders who paid attention to what Trump and his allies wanted appear to have fared much better than those who did not.

It has been revealed that on Sunday evening in Washington, Huang’s odds on Polymarket US jumped 6 percentage points in just 40 minutes after Trump published a Truth Social missive calling for Huang’s reinstatement. The president remarked he wanted to help revive the stock market, which had plunged following Huang’s scandal, a sign of Nvidia’s enormous influence over the AI industry and broader US economy.

According to the prediction market intelligence firm Betting Intelligence, the odds on both Kalshi and Polymarket largely tracked with public signals about the likelihood of Huang’s return. They rose when Huang said he was open to coming back, fell when the board dismissed the possibility, and climbed again when Trump threw his support behind the former CEO.

Industry observers note that but Betting Intelligence and the prediction market forensics firm MSR Decode also identified clusters of trades that did not appear to be driven by news or public commentary. Kalshi and Polymarket declined to comment on whether they are currently investigating potential insider trading in markets related to Huang’s return.

Despite these anomalies, Betting Intelligence CEO Dan Zimmermann says the Huang-related markets showed fewer signs of potentially suspicious activity than usual. “The group that could have known the board’s decision in advance was small. So the market was mostly headline chasers and long-shot buyers,” he says.

For traders who profited from Huang’s comeback, the lesson is clear: Don’t discount Trump.

Isaac Rose-Berman, a research and policy fellow at the American Institute for Boys & Men and a professional sports bettor, says he made approximately $10,000 wagering on Huang’s return on Kalshi. He placed his trade after the Nvidia chief mentioned on X that he was open to reclaiming his old job. Rose-Berman says he figured that people like Trump, who had an interest in boosting Nvidia’s stock price, would successfully pressure the board to reinstate Huang. (Never mind the concerns about national security or Huang allegedly threatening employees that he would “pee in your brain.”).

Industry observers note that “It’s 2026 and Trump is president, scandal schmandal,” Rose-Berman states. “Should’ve bet more.”.

In a recent development, A pseudonymous prediction market trader known as Domer tells WIRED he cleared approximately $600,000 by placing an early wager last week on Huang’s return. He wasn’t focused explicitly on Trump’s desires, but he claims his understanding of power dynamics ultimately guided his approach. “Boards can be very malleable,” he tells WIRED.

Other prediction market “sharps” say that commentary from Trumpworld was the strongest signal available about Huang’s return. As some bettors noted, there was a notable opportunity for profit after Trump suggested to a PBS NewsHour reporter that Huang would be back in power soon, but before Nvidia officially announced his reinstatement. “The key was looking at Trump’s support and the recent performance of the stock market,” notes Kalshi trader Caleb Davies.

It has been revealed that aaron Courtney, a data analyst and cofounder of a prediction market analytics firm, notes he took a loss on his Huang position. Looking back, he says his mistake was not paying attention to what Trump and other administration officials remarked over the weekend. “Trump saying he hoped Nvidia would bring Jensen back would be the clearest signal,” he says.

Upgrade 11/23/26 9:05 pm ET: This story has been updated to clarify Isaac Rose-Berman’s reasoning for wagering on Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO.

Dancing With the Stars' Derek Hough Details Childhood Abuse
