💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the Dancing With the Stars judge looked back on the beginning of his path to becoming a professional dancer, he shared one of the darker chapters of his childhood with sister Julianne Hough while being raised in the suburbs of Salt Lake City, Utah.
  • "The neighborhood that we grew up in, we definitely just had some neighbors that weren't great.
  • In addition, the 41-year-old explained of the traumatic period, "They hung me up in a tree by my ankles, put a gun to my head, spat on me, hogtied me up in a field and left me there.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Derek Hough healed through dance.

As the Dancing With the Stars judge looked back on the beginning of his path to becoming a professional dancer, he shared one of the darker chapters of his childhood with sister Julianne Hough while being raised in the suburbs of Salt Lake City, Utah.

"The neighborhood that we grew up in, we definitely just had some neighbors that weren't great. They pretty much terrorized my family in a lot of ways," Derek shared in his Nov. 23 documentary Symphony of Dance per USA Today, stating, "One of my neighbors was, for lack of a better word, just really inappropriate with me physically.".

In addition, the 41-year-old explained of the traumatic period, "They hung me up in a tree by my ankles, put a gun to my head, spat on me, hogtied me up in a field and left me there.".

It has been revealed that as such, enduring the abuse led to "a lot of emotion" for the then-12-year-old, who was raised alongside his DWTS costar as well as their older siblings Sharee, 49, Marabeth, 45 and Katherine, 44, by parents Bruce Hough and Mariann Heaton in the Mormon community. Julianne has previously shared that a painful part of her upbringing came at the hands of a neighbor in their cul-de-sac who she said sexually abused her at age 4.

"I just didn't understand where I was going," Derek stated in the Hulu project about his reaction to the harmful treatment. "I was kind of left to my own devices.".

And at first, the trauma pushed the choreographer further away from his future as a ballroom pro.

As he detailed, "I was a 12-year-old. I would skip school. I would skip dance. I wouldn't go. My dad was at work, and my mom was off, and [I was] just floating around with no direction.".

Fortunately, Derek was "relieved" when he met mentors Corky Ballas and Shirley Ballas—parents of DWTS coach Mark Ballas—who soon moved Derek, and eventually Julianne, to London to attend drama academy Italia Conti Academy of Theatre Arts.

"Moving away was great because I was getting away from something," he said. "I was leaving this wounded boy, and I was gonna go become this success. I was gonna go work hard and achieve things and overcome things.".

And the Emmy winner did exactly that, noting how the professional performers in his upcoming world made him realize at the time, "This is what I want to do. I want to be like these guys.".

In a recent development, julianne alluded to her siblings undergoing hardship similar to her own on The Jamie Kern Lima Show Aug. 15 while telling her story, noting, "By the way, I'm not the only one in my family that had gone through similar things, so that was a very challenging thing to come to terms with.".

Read on for a closer look at the Hough family tree.

The Hough family patriarch is originally from Coeur d’Alene, Idaho, and met future wife Mariann Heaton on the ballroom team at Ricks College (now Brigham Young University-Idaho).

Industry observers note that bruce and Mariann—both from Mormon families and the children of ballroom-dancing parents—settled in Salt Lake City. There he worked as a communications executive and co-founded supplement maker Nutraceutical Corporation, which, according to Deseret News, reached a valuation of $300 million under his watch before it was sold in 2017.

Bruce also ventured into politics, serving two terms as state Republican Party chair and running for congress in 2023.

Sources indicate that while he didn't win that race, he told Deseret News at the time that he was running for his family's future. "I’ve got 10 kids, I’ve got 22 grandkids and growing," he explained. "And I really feel that America’s promise is in jeopardy for those grandkids especially.".

Of his most famous offspring, he quipped, "I never thought that those dance lessons would pay off,” noting that he took the most pride in hearing from others that son Derek Hough and daughter Julianne Hough were some of the "kindest people…in the entertainment business.”.

According to recent reports, in addition to Derek and Julianne, Bruce shares daughters Sharee Hough Selman, Marabeth Poole and Katherine Hough with Mariann. After they divorced in the late 1990s, he married Debra Francom Hough, also a parent of five.

Mariann grew up in Idaho Falls with three brothers.

She and Bruce were in the process of divorcing when Julianne and Derek, then 10 and 13, moved to London to attend the Italia Conti Academy of Theatre Arts.

According to recent reports, their leaving was "devastating," Mariann recalled on a 2019 episode of The Minds Gym podcast. But they wanted to dance and, she explained, "The biggest thing that kept me going is that I grew up feeling very dominated over and controlled. Love my parents, but that was like a generational thing.".

However, she added, "I'm grateful for that now because…it made me sway to I love having free agency." It was also "so crucial" for her to pass that on to her kids, she said, and "all of them are so not afraid to go travel and do all these things.".

Mariann, now based in Franklin, Tenn., is a painter and has credited husband Aaron Nelson for supporting and encouraging her work as an artist.

Sharee married husband Mark Selman when she was 19 and they share six kids.

The eldest of Bruce and Mariann's brood danced at Ballet West in Utah and these days runs her own fitness business, Hough Werks, teaching yoga and dance.

Her "dynamic" firstborn "just came into this world with a lot of energy," Mariann noted on The Minds Gym. Sharee's "little mind was just going all the time, just super creative" and "self-motivated.".

Moreover, with 11 years between Sharee and her youngest sister, "Julianne thinks she has two moms.".

Marabeth is "just a beautiful spirit" who "loves her own space," Mariann said of her second child, and she "puts on these little retreats in Nashville for women.".

She left Utah for Music City to "be a country star," baby sister Julianne shared on the Not Skinny but Not Fat podcast in September 2025, and now makes the most of her positive energy as a realtor and holistic health coach, as well as a singer-songwriter.

Marabeth married Michael Poole in 2002 and they live in Nashville with son Aidan.

Daughter Katherine, a mother of three, "just makes you smile," Mariann said on The Minds Gym, "and she's just real.".

Industry observers note that the esthetician was in a relationship with Tony Schnur before his death from brain cancer in 2023. "It’s unfair that I found my soulmate, my best friend, my partner in life, only to lose you too soon," Katherine posted on Instragram in February 2025, marking the second anniversary of his passing. "I miss you every day.".

But Katherine has persevered, Julianne gushing on Not Skinny But Not Fat, "She has three beautiful daughters and she has all these activities and she plans all these things, and I'm in awe of her.".

Recent findings suggest that and on Sept. 24, 2025, Katherine shared that she had found love again, writing on Instagram alongside a montage of sweet photos, "After walking through so much loss and heartache, I never imagined I’d find this kind of love again. Chris is the man I prayed for, kind, generous, loving, patient, and such a gift not only to me but to my girls.".

Born May 17, 1985, Derek joined Dancing With the Stars as a pro in 2007. He won the Mirrorball Trophy a record six times and is a four-time Emmy winner for choreography.

After his last competitive turn around the floor in 2016, Derek returned to DWTS as a fulltime judge in 2020.

He met fellow dancer Hayley Erbert in 2015 and, after navigating some "insane obstacles," as he put it on Couple Things With Shawn Johnson and Andrew East, they got married in August 2023.

As a couple they powered through Hayley's life-threatening health scare, a brain hemorrhage that required emergency surgery just four months after their wedding, and in July 2025 they revealed they were expecting their first child together.

Sources indicate that posting a photo of dad Bruce dancing at his and Hayley's wedding, Derek wrote on Facebook in April 2024, "Smart, kind and thoughtful. I hope to be as good as a father as he has been to his family.".

Industry observers note that the baby of the Hough family was born July 20,1988. She joined DWTS in 2007 along with Derek and proceeded to win her first two seasons on the show.

She left in 2009 to pursue acting and scored a breakthrough role in 2010's Burlesque (though her substantial-screen debut was actually playing an unnamed Hogwarts student in 2001's Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone) before scoring the lead in the 2011 Footloose remake. Julianne returned to the ballroom as a judge from 2014 to 2017, winning an Emmy for choreography along the way, and has cohosted DWTS with Alfonso Ribeiro since 2023.

Julianne married Brooks Laich in 2017 but they split up in 2020, eventually finalizing their divorce in 2022.

She mentioned on The Jamie Kern Lima Show in 2024 that going through a divorce gave her a chance to "reconnect" with her mom and dad, and they "showed up" for her.

"I needed that," Julianne explained. "I reclaimed my parental relationship with them and I got to be the kid and they got to take care of me. And that was the most healing [thing].".

Reflecting on her and Derek becoming the stars of the family, Julianne said on Not Skinny But Not Fat that there was "no jealousy" between their other siblings, "but there is a sadness that maybe there wasn't an opportunity for them to experience it.".

Sharee, Marabeth and Katherine are "so, so, so happy," Julianne continued. "They have great lives, and they love their life. But we had an opportunity that they didn't have, and it's hard.”.

Sources indicate that and while she and Derek have a special connection, "they were super close as sisters growing up,” Julianne stated. “So, I didn't get to have the closeness of sisters and that bond. [And] they have marriages and kids and I don't have that experience.".

Meanwhile, all five siblings "get along really well," Mariann mentioned on The Minds Gym. "I think the hard part is being away from each other, because there is some kind of a synergy when they all get together.".

#173619. Breaking: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1150 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1150 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that exercising too intensely without enough recovery time may affect more than muscles and physical endurance.
  • In a newly introduced study published in the journal Neuroscience, researchers in Brazil found that prolonged, exhausting exercise altered dopamine regulation in the hippocampus, a brain region important for memory and emotional regulation.
  • The scientists observed that mice exposed to demanding exercise schedules continued to have elevated dopamine levels during periods when they should have been recovering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that exercising too intensely without enough recovery time may affect more than muscles and physical endurance. New research suggests that excessive training can also disrupt brain chemistry, potentially interfering with the processes that help the brain return to its normal resting state.

In a newly introduced study published in the journal Neuroscience, researchers in Brazil found that prolonged, exhausting exercise altered dopamine regulation in the hippocampus, a brain region important for memory and emotional regulation.

The scientists observed that mice exposed to demanding exercise schedules continued to have elevated dopamine levels during periods when they should have been recovering. Dopamine plays an crucial role in motivation and alertness, and the researchers believe that similar disruptions in humans could help explain why excessive training is sometimes associated with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue. If confirmed, this connection would provide further evidence that sufficient rest is essential for both physical fitness and mental well-being.

"Our findings show that excessive physical exercise affects not only skeletal muscle but also has a pronounced impact on the brain," said Alisson Luiz da Rocha, the study's first author.

Rocha carried out the research during his doctoral studies at the Ribeirão Preto School of Physical Education and Sports at the University of São Paulo (EEFERP-USP) in Brazil, supported by a scholarship from FAPESP. He explained that the findings demonstrate how exercise influences the central nervous system, with effects extending well beyond muscle development.

How Scientists Simulated Overtraining.

To investigate what happens in the brain when exercise becomes excessive, the team studied two main groups of mice exposed to different levels of physical activity.

One group completed a single strenuous treadmill session, running until they reached exhaustion. The other followed an extended training program designed to reproduce the demanding conditions associated with overtraining syndrome in elite athletes.

Overtraining syndrome occurs when the physical demands of training exceed the body's ability to recover. It can cause declining athletic performance, reduced appetite, ongoing fatigue, muscle pain, and a greater risk of injuries. Changes in immune function and metabolism are also common.

Industry observers note that for the extended training experiment, the mice exercised over eight weeks as the researchers gradually increased the workload. By the final week, they were completing two sessions each day, with only four hours of recovery between workouts.

According to recent reports, after the exercise programs, the scientists examined the animals' hippocampi. They measured dopamine and serotonin, along with proteins involved in producing and managing these chemical messengers. These included tyrosine hydroxylase (TyrH), an enzyme needed for dopamine production, and vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2), which helps package neurotransmitters for release.

Dopamine Remained Elevated for 48 Hours.

According to recent reports, in mice that completed just one exhausting treadmill session, dopamine levels increased shortly after exercise. This showed that even a single bout of intense activity could produce a measurable chemical response in the brain.

Sources indicate that the more striking results came from the animals that underwent weeks of demanding training. In this group, both dopamine and TyrH remained elevated for 48 hours after the performance test, even though the mice were in their recovery period.

It has been revealed that this prolonged response suggests that repeated strenuous exercise without sufficient rest may interfere with the brain's normal regulation of dopamine. Rather than swiftly returning to its usual chemical state, the brain continued to show signs of altered neurotransmitter activity long after the exercise had ended.

Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva, a professor at EEFERP-USP who coordinated the study, explained that finding comparable changes in humans could help researchers better understand the possible connections between overtraining, brain chemistry, and sleep disturbances.

Recent findings suggest that however, the researchers caution that the study did not directly measure sleep, anxiety, or alertness. Those possible consequences remain to be investigated, and additional research is needed to determine whether the same dopamine changes occur in people.

According to recent reports, dopamine is often associated with pleasure and motivation, but it also helps regulate wakefulness and other essential brain functions. Its presence is not harmful on its own. What matters is whether its activity remains appropriately balanced.

According to Rocha, difficulties could arise if dopamine remains unusually elevated when the brain should be preparing for sleep. Such changes could also disrupt the balance between dopamine and other neurotransmitters, potentially affecting how the nervous system regulates activity and rest.

Another notable finding involved serotonin, a neurotransmitter that has long been investigated for its possible role in fatigue. Despite the substantial changes in dopamine, the researchers detected no significant differences in serotonin levels between the animals.

This result challenges the long-standing idea that serotonin alone is primarily responsible for excessive fatigue. Instead, the findings suggest that changes in dopamine regulation may also deserve attention when scientists investigate the biological effects of overtraining.

Why Recovery Is Essential for the Brain and Body.

Although the connection between these chemical changes and symptoms such as insomnia or anxiety has not yet been established in humans, the findings reinforce the importance of allowing sufficient time for recovery.

Excessive training without adequate rest can undermine the benefits of exercise, contributing to reduced performance, persistent muscle pain, and problems with immune function. The fresh results suggest that changes in brain chemistry may be another important part of this process.

For recreational exercisers and professional athletes alike, the researchers emphasize that training should be balanced with appropriate recovery and expert guidance. Increasing workout intensity does not necessarily produce better results if the body is not given enough time to adapt.

Rocha also conducted research during a postdoctoral fellowship at the School of Applied Sciences (FCA) of the State University of Campinas (UNICAMP) in Limeira. This work included an internship at the University of Michigan in the United States, where he at the moment works as a researcher.

Recent findings suggest that additional funding came from a Thematic Project led by Silva, a postdoctoral fellowship awarded to Ana Paula Pinto, and a direct doctorate scholarship supporting João Pedro Floriano. Both Pinto and Floriano are affiliated with EEFERP-USP.

Recent findings suggest that the team is now participating in a newly introduced international research project aimed at identifying which biological systems first begin to show signs of strain when exercise exceeds the level at which it normally produces beneficial adaptations. Understanding these early warning signals could help scientists determine when productive training begins to become harmful.

After working 9 to 5 on the Friday of Stagecoach weekend, country music fans will be able to enjoy a whole day devoted to Dolly Parton at the country music festival next year.

It has been revealed that as revealed Monday (Nov. 23) on The Voice, the first day of the three-day festival will officially be known as Dolly Day. Host Carson Daly explained on the singing competition show that Stagecoach will encourage guests to wear their Parton “gear” before throwing it over to coach Riley Green, who showed off his tee emblazoned with the late country icon’s image.

Recent findings suggest that green will headline next year’s Stagecoach, which also features fellow Voice coach Kelly Clarkson on the lineup. She teased, “You should show ’em what the shirt really looks like.”.

As a few ladies in the crowd squealed loudly, Green tastefully lifted his hoodie slightly to show that his Parton shirt had nothing by way of sleeves, giving the crowd a narrow glimpse of his biceps.

Recent findings suggest that stagecoach will take place April 23-25 in Indio, Calif. Garth Brooks and Zach Top are also among the headliners, leading a bill that features HARDY, Turnpike Troubadours, Charley Crockett, Jo Dee Messina, Kaitlin Butts, Willie Nelson & Family, Kelly Clarkson, Brothers Osborne, Shaboozey, Dasha, Stella Lefty and more.

Industry observers note that it’ll mark the first year of the country fest since Parton died at the age of 80 in August following a cancer battle. About a month afterward the icon’s passing, Clarkson opened up about a meaningful moment she shared with the Queen of Country on the day of the 2023 ACM Awards, where the two women performed a duet of “I Will Always Love You” at the ACM Awards. Just 30 minutes before they went on stage, Clarkson learned that her divorce from ex-husband Brandon Blackstock — who died three years later — had been finalized.

Sources indicate that “I found out right before that performance,” Clarkson stated on Las Culturistas in September. “She, kind of, caught me. I was like, ‘I’m sorry. It’s just kind of a wild moment for me.’ We just had this moment … What she said backstage to me, it was just a really beautiful thing.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX set a new record with its latest satellite launch out of California.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Launch Complex-4E on Sunday (Nov. 22) at 7:23 a.m. ET (1223 GMT; 4:23 a.m. local time in California), on a mission for the U.S. National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) called NROL-136.

In a recent development, it was the second launch from that pad in a little over 32 hours, after the USSF-317 mission for the U.S. Space Force. And that quick turnaround made history.

Recent findings suggest that massive high five to the @SpaceX west coast team for a world record launch to launch turn from Pad 4e last night! 32 hr, 3 min, 21 sec! This smashed the previous record of 45 hrs from Pad 40. Team got there with several hours of margin. Next goal… the 24 hr turn! 🏎️🚀🏎️🚀November 22, 2026.

In a recent development, "Massive high five to the @SpaceX west coast team for a world record launch to launch turn from Pad 4e last night! 32 hr, 3 min, 21 sec! This smashed the previous record of 45 hrs from Pad 40. Team got there with several hours of margin. Next goal… the 24 hr turn!" Kiko Dontchev, SpaceX's vice president of launch, said via X on Sunday. (Pad 40 is at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.).

Industry observers note that NROL-136 was the sixth launch of 2026 so far for the NRO. All of them have been carried out by SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9, and all have delivered classified satellites to low Earth orbit.

The launch marked another step in the NRO's effort to expand its intelligence-gathering capabilities through a proliferated network of spacecraft designed to provide more frequent and timely surveillance of locations around the globe.

Sources indicate that about two minutes after liftoff, the Falcon 9's first-stage booster separated from the rocket's upper stage, which continued carrying the classified payloads onward to orbit. The booster then reversed course and returned to Vandenberg, touching down at Landing Zone 4 approximately seven and a half minutes after launch.

Saturday's launch was the 14th flight for this particular Falcon 9 booster, dubbed B1097, which previously launched NASA's Sentinel-6B ocean-monitoring satellite, NROL-172, USSF-259 for the Space Force, and eight Starlink missions.

NROL-136 was the 15th launch dedicated to building the NRO's "proliferated architecture," the satellites for which have been developed in partnership with SpaceX and Northrop Grumman. The network is designed to increase coverage and improve the "capability and resilience" of U.S. intelligence operations in space, according to the NRO's mission website.

It has been revealed that the NRO began deploying the constellation in May 2024 with the launch of NROL-146. The most recent proliferated architecture mission before Sunday was NROL-179, which lifted off on June 19, 2026.

As with any classified mission, the agency has not disclosed the exact number of satellites aboard NROL-136 or revealed details about their onboard technologies.

Recent findings suggest that editor's note: This story was updated at 11 p.m. ET on Nov. 22 with the news that NROL-136 set a newly introduced record for the shortest time between two introduces from the same pad.

Tech Report: U.S. officially loses measles elimination status amid ongoing outbreaks

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the U.S.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Pan American Health Organization declared the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence.
  • In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking latest ones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the U.S. on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus.

Recent findings suggest that the Pan American Health Organization declared the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence. The director of PAHO, the regional branch of the World Health Organization, made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission.

In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking latest ones.

In a recent development, "The commission concluded that endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn — a recommendation which I have accepted," Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO director, said during a news briefing on Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that it's a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates and vaccine hesitancy fuel outbreaks across the country that have sickened thousands of people and led to a tragic string of preventable deaths. Among the deaths where vaccination status was reported, all were unvaccinated.

According to recent reports, more than 5,400 measles cases had been reported nationwide in 2026 as of mid-November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. States have confirmed 10 deaths associated with the disease so far in 2026: seven in Pennsylvania, one in New York and two in Wisconsin.

The commission found that out of 52 U.S. states and territories it tracked, 48 experienced measles outbreaks during the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, PAHO Assistant Director Dr. Rhonda Sealey-Thomas mentioned during the briefing. But Barbosa said the countries are already taking action to control outbreaks, such as strengthening vaccination, surveillance for timely case detection and outbreak response efforts.

Industry observers note that the U.S. in particular has ramped up vaccination efforts to close immunity gaps, particularly in areas with low immunization coverage experiencing outbreaks, noted Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO's Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. He said PAHO expects the U.S. to present its corrective action blueprint in the coming weeks, outlining strategies to regain its designation.

In a Tuesday release, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it will continue to ensure all communities have the resources to prevent and respond to outbreaks and is committed to working with states and other local partners to restore the U.S.'s measles elimination status.

It has been revealed that CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz stated in the release that the measles elimination designation "is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does." She said the agency has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach communities where transmission is occurring.

It has been revealed that last week, Schwartz told Reuters that the agency is going to be "doing the same exact thing that we've been doing today" if the U.S. loses its measles-free status.

It has been revealed that the decision also poses a new test for the Trump administration and its Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has taken steps to change recommendations for the childhood measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine and has a long history of questioning its safety without evidence.

But Kennedy, in a Tuesday X post, said he continues to recommend MMR vaccination as "the most effective way to prevent measles.".

"We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," Kennedy stated. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment.".

Industry observers note that CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation's public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. The resurgence of measles exposes eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities.

Public health experts previously told CNBC that the return of measles ultimately boils down to fewer children getting vaccinated.

According to recent reports, the MMR vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the CDC. Yet data aggregated by the CDC demonstrates that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission.

The American Medical Association urged the public to get vaccinated after PAHO's announcement.

"We must treat the current measles outbreaks as an urgent call to rebuild trust in science-based recommendations and restore strong, fully-funded public health infrastructure to protect families and communities and prevent the return of diseases once eliminated," AMA President Dr. Willie Underwood said in a statement.

In a separate statement, the pharmaceutical industry's largest lobbying group called on policymakers to provide "clear, accurate information about the seriousness of measles infection and the effectiveness of vaccines against it, restore and sustain high vaccination coverage in every community, strengthen vaccination efforts, and invest in disease surveillance and rapid outbreak response.".

Recent findings suggest that "We have the tools to eliminate measles again and what we need now is the commitment to use them," mentioned Dr. Michael Ybarra, chief medical officer of the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America.

Measles isn't just a public health threat — it's also a huge financial burden on the healthcare system, CNBC reported.

In a recent development, based on this year's case count, a fresh tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses.

Sources indicate that the U.S. now joins Canada, Spain and the U.K., which all recently lost their measles-free status after a review by experts at the World Health Organization. While the U.S. dropped out of the WHO, it remains a member of PAHO, its Americas branch.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you thought the Jensen Huang saga was over when he stepped down as Nvidia's CEO, think again. Less than two weeks later, Nvidia gave him his job back.

And within hours of Monday's surprise announcement, senators set a date to question him in public — and under oath.

In a recent development, huang, who co-founded chipmaker Nvidia, is scheduled to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Thursday, Dec. 3, at 10 a.m. ET, just two days after he's scheduled to speak with various committees of the U.S. House of Representatives. He’s the only witness listed for the hearing, which will focus on U.S. rules limiting where companies can sell their most advanced AI chips. If you want to watch, the committee will be livestreaming the hearing on its website.

Huang has already returned to the Nvidia office, where he was welcomed by cheering employees.

"I'm going to be a better CEO the second time around," he told workers, as seen in a video on X.

Meanwhile, President Trump is taking personal credit for negotiating Huang's return to Nvidia. In a Truth Social post, the president stated he assured the Nvidia board that Huang did not pose a national security risk.

President Trump also posted a picture of Jensen Huang photoshopped into his assassination attempt scene while holding up a red bra with an Nvidia flag in the background. Yes, really.

Recent findings suggest that the questions about Nvidia's chips go back well before Huang initially stepped down. In 2024, federal investigators began looking into whether Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer based in Singapore, had sent advanced AI chips to China in violation of U.S. export rules. That investigation took on upcoming significance when reports surfaced that Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, who used to run Megaspeed. Jensen Huang acknowledged the affair, and U.S. authorities suspect Alice Huang of working for Chinese intelligence, according to the New York Times (though China has since denied that she was a spy).

It has been revealed that the newly empowered House Democrats also have questions for Huang, including whether Nvidia interfered with that investigation. In a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, they asked whether his department had allowed Nvidia to intervene in the Megaspeed probe. Lawmakers are also looking into exactly how Huang got his job back and what role the Trump administration played.

Just days before Nvidia brought him back, the board had made clear it had no intends to reinstate him, despite Huang saying he would be "honored" to return. On the manufacturer's earnings call on Nov. 17, board chair Harvey Jones even stated, "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.".

Yet, on Nov. 23, the board voted unanimously to do just that. In a statement, the board wrote that it had heard from senior U.S. officials, and "based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk.".

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Harvey Jones remarked in the statement.

Trump had already signaled he was open to Huang getting his job back. On Nov. 16, he told reporters he "would not mind" if Huang returned as CEO and stated Huang had "learned a major lesson.".

In a recent development, by Monday, Trump was taking credit for the decision. He told CNBC he'd pushed Nvidia's board to bring Huang back. Asked whether the board would have done so without him, Trump mentioned, "The answer is no. I believe my intervention was very important." He also posted on Truth Social, writing, "The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO… Congratulations to Jensen, the NVIDIA Board, to the People of the United States — and, indeed, the World!".

That leaves lawmakers in both parties asking what changed. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) called the decision "reckless" and asked the administration to name the officials who spoke to Nvidia and explain what they told the board. Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) asked, "No national security risk? Based on what?" he wrote on X.

In a recent development, huang had already agreed to answer questions from House lawmakers before he got his job back. That interview is still set for Tuesday, Dec. 1, two days before the public Senate hearing. He’ll meet with three House committees behind closed doors, and the interview will be transcribed.

In a recent development, but now, Huang could also be answering a new set of questions in public about the affair that helped cost him his job and the president who says he got it back for him. So far, Nvidia and Trump have told their sides of the story. The hearing is a chance to hear Huang's.

Tom Brady knows that all parents drop the ball sometimes.

Since becoming dad to son Jack, 19, with ex-girlfriend Bridget Moynahan, as well as son Benjamin, 16, and daughter Vivian, 13, with ex-wife Gisele Bündchen, the seven-time Super Bowl champ admitted there are some losses among his many wins as a parent.

And with that effort, the 49-year-old added, “I hope I’m a better parent today than I was when I first started having kids. And hopefully I’m a better parent 10 years from now.”.

So, what is Brady’s game plan for becoming the best dad he can be?

“The important thing for me in my personal life is to go where my kids are at, too,” he explained. “Not to say, ‘Hey kids, pay attention to the things I'm doing or what's important to me.’ It’s been a really important lesson for me over the years to go to my kids and say, ‘What’s really important to you? What’s driving you? Or what are you scared of, or how can I pay attention to the things that you value?’”.

Finding ways to connect with his kids is a skill Brady noted he developed from leading football teams during his 23 seasons as an NFL quarterback.

“Part of that is just being really open and present and also trying to be really relatable to the younger [generation],” he continued, “which I was very fortunate to learn over the course of my playing career.”.

And now, Brady emphasized that he is simply trying to be “really present” and “non-judgmental” with his kids while imparting the wisdom he’s scored through his “years of experience.”.

As he put it, he is “just trying to understand their perspective, but also trying to get them to understand my perspective a little bit, too.”.

Last week, Greene’s Twitter account was temporarily suspended by the Elon Musk-headed platform over a tweet with a graphic referring to a “Trans Day of Vengeance,” as she denounced a planned transgender rights rally.

And come Tuesday, Greene has confirmed looks to protest in New York City when former President Donald Trump is expected to be arraigned on an indictment of more than 30 counts, calling the proceedings against him an “unconstitutional WITCH HUNT!”.

In a recent development, but on Sunday, Greene was featured on CBS’ “60 Minutes” in an interview the long-running show promoted on Twitter with the tease: “Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, nicknamed MTG, isn’t afraid to share her opinions, no matter how intense and in-your-face they are. She sits down with Lesley Stahl this Sunday on 60 Minutes.” The images attached to this tweet by “60 Minutes” include Greene and Stahl walking through the US Capitol, taking a stroll outside and Greene showing Stahl something on her phone.

It's time for Marjorie Taylor Greene to go.

In the segment that aired Sunday night, Stahl noted the congresswoman had moved from the fringe to the GOP’s front row in two years despite a “sharp tongue” and “some pretty radical views” as well as “over the top” comments such as “the Democrats are a party of pedophiles.” Stahl also referred to video of Greene chasing a Parkland, Florida, school shooting survivor, still maintaining that the 2020 election was stolen and failing to criticize Trump over spending. (The interview was conducted before news of his indictment.).

But Stahl didn’t mention Greene spoke at a white nationalist event a year ago while a member of Congress or her extreme anti-Muslim views and her defense of January 6 rioters.

Criticism of CBS for amplifying Greene has been swift and well-deserved even before the program aired. Former GOP Rep. Adam Kinzinger of Illinois tweeted beforehand: “Wow. Insane that 60 min would do this.” (Kinzinger is a CNN senior political commentator.).

Journalist Molly Jong-Fast also slammed “60 Minutes” with the tweet: “Attention is currency and 60 minutes is spending its currency on the Jewish space lasers woman.” (Jong-Fast was apparently referring to Greene’s past claim that a massive California wildfire was started by “a laser” beamed from space controlled by a prominent Jewish banking family.).

David Hogg, who survived the 2018 horrific school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland and has since become an activist against gun violence, responded, “I look forward to your questions about why she thinks school shootings are fake and why she’s supported QAnon.”.

Trump's risky call for protests.

Greene amplified the conspiracy theory — two years before being elected to Congress — that the Parkland shooting that took 17 lives was staged. And in 2019, Greene appeared on video confronting Hogg outside the Capitol when he was championing laws to save lives from gun violence, screaming that the then-teenager was a “coward.” She also called Hogg “#littleHitler” on social media.

Greene’s own tweet promoting Sunday’s segment was not filled with her typical smears of “fake news” when she doesn’t like the coverage. Rather, Greene urged people to tune in as she praised “60 Minutes” host Stahl (and misspelled her first name): “It was an honor to spend a few days with the legendary icon Leslie Stahl and talented crew @60Minutes.” Greene added, “Leslie is a trailblazer for women in journalism. And while we may disagree on some concerns, I respect her greatly.”.

Industry observers note that now, it is true that “60 Minutes” over its 50-plus-year history has featured what the show has dubbed “controversial” guests. These include a 2000 interview with Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, whose 1995 terrorist attack left 168 dead, including 19 children. And the show did a 1979 interview with Iran’s Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

According to recent reports, perhaps “60 Minutes” views Greene — who has repeatedly downplayed and even defended the January 6, 2021, attack plus called for the GOP to become the party of “Christian nationalism” — in the vein of its long list of controversial guests. (CBS had not responded to a request from CNN for comment at time of publishing.).

Join us on Twitter and Facebook.

However, the choice of Greene as a guest instantly recalls the comments of then-CBS CEO Les Moonves during Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign when he admitted that Trump’s candidacy “may not be good for America, but it’s damn good for CBS.” Moonves added, “The money’s rolling in and this is fun. … (T)his is going to be a very good year for us,” concluding, “Sorry. It’s a terrible thing to say. But bring it on, Donald. Keep going.”.

Moonves may be gone from CBS, but it appears his mindset continues at “60 Minutes.” And that may be good for “60 Minutes,” but it’s definitely not good for America.

#173612. Industry News: This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs

Industry News: This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (923 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A fossil discovered in Illinois years ago has turned out to belong to a previously unrecognized species that lived 309 million years ago, long before dinosaurs appeared.
  • During the Carboniferous period, the region surrounding present-day Chicago looked dramatically different.
  • It has been revealed that the newly identified species, Jeanerpeton mazonensis, resembled a salamander with the short, stocky body of a frog.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A fossil discovered in Illinois years ago has turned out to belong to a previously unrecognized species that lived 309 million years ago, long before dinosaurs appeared. The strange animal, an early relative of modern amphibians, has also received a name with a personal connection to the two student scientists who helped identify it.

During the Carboniferous period, the region surrounding present-day Chicago looked dramatically different. Instead of a modern city, the landscape was a warm, swampy river delta populated by giant insects, early animals adapted to life on land, and unusual creatures swimming through its waterways. This environment supported an extraordinary variety of life, leaving behind fossils that now provide a remarkable glimpse into Earth's prehistoric past.

It has been revealed that the newly identified species, Jeanerpeton mazonensis, resembled a salamander with the short, stocky body of a frog. Its name means "Jean's crawler from Mazon Creek," honoring the mothers of the two student researchers, both of whom are named Jean. The discovery is described in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.

A 309-Million-Year-Old Fossil With Extraordinary Detail.

The Mazon Creek fossil deposits are among the world's most key sources of Carboniferous fossils, in large part because of the conditions that existed when the animals were alive.

As plants and animals died in the ancient river delta, layers of sediment swiftly covered their remains. This rapid burial created ideal conditions for fossilization, sometimes preserving delicate structures that would ordinarily disappear long before they could become fossils.

"What's really cool about Mazon Creek is that it preserves all of these unusual details -- things like toe pads and body outlines," says Allison Sefcovic, co-lead author of the paper and 2025 Women in Science intern at the Field.

"In the fossil of Jeanerpeton, we can see some of the scales on its back and tiny 'belly ribs' called gastralia. You can even see the eye impressions! It's so cool to see.".

These exceptionally preserved features offer valuable evidence of what early amphibian relatives looked like. They also indicate that several anatomical characteristics associated with modern frogs and salamanders were already present approximately 309 million years ago.

A Prehistoric Species Hidden in Plain Sight.

It has been revealed that although Jeanerpeton mazonensis has only recently been formally described, its fossil was discovered many years earlier. An amateur fossil collector originally found the specimen and later donated it to the Field Museum.

When researchers first examined it, they classified the animal as Amphibamus grandiceps, a previously established species known from the Mazon Creek area. However, closer examination eventually revealed that the fossil represented a distinct animal.

Misidentifications like this can occur when scientists have limited information about ancient species. Fossils that appear similar are sometimes assigned to an existing species even when notable differences have not yet been recognized.

Paleontologists refer to such broad classifications as a "waste bin taxon." The term describes a category in which multiple fossils are grouped together because they seem related, even though their true identities and evolutionary relationships remain poorly understood.

"What we're finding from the Field Museum's collection are a bunch of things that historically were grouped together into this waste bin taxon known as Amphibamus grandiceps," says Cam So, co-author on the study and postdoctoral researcher at the Field Museum.

"Jeanerpeton is one of those species. And now, we've found enough evidence to support it being an anatomically distinct animal. With this publication, we officially pull Jeanerpeton out of this waste bin taxon.".

The finding highlights how museum collections can continue to produce discoveries long after fossils are first collected. In this case, a specimen already held by the Field Museum provided enough anatomical evidence to establish a separate species.

Two Student Scientists Make a Remarkable Discovery.

According to recent reports, the research was co-led by Payton Kohlberg and Allison Sefcovic, who participated in the Field Museum's Women in Science internship program in 2025. The initiative encourages young women to explore careers in scientific research and museums.

Both students worked alongside So as members of the research group led by Arjan Mann, the museum's assistant curator of fossil fishes and early tetrapods in the Negaunee Integrative Research Center.

For Kohlberg, the project offered an opportunity to enter an unfamiliar scientific field and gain confidence through hands-on research.

"Before working in the Mann Lab, I didn't know much about paleontology," states Kohlberg. "My experience at the Field and in the Women in Science program has made me more confident in my abilities to try something upcoming. It is scary to take on a project when you feel like you don't know as much as you should, but I learned with my practical experience that it is possible to overcome that fear with hard work.".

According to recent reports, the identification of Jeanerpeton mazonensis adds another species to the growing record of ancient life preserved at Mazon Creek. As researchers continue examining fossils from the region, each discovery helps reveal more about the extraordinary diversity of animals and plants that inhabited Illinois more than 300 million years ago.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that jensen Huang received a “hero’s welcome” from employees on Monday after Nvidia’s board of directors reinstated him as CEO, according to people who were present.
  • But other employees were quietly stewing.
  • Industry observers note that some employees were alarmed by Huang’s alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a subordinate and another with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that jensen Huang received a “hero’s welcome” from employees on Monday after Nvidia’s board of directors reinstated him as CEO, according to people who were present. An outspoken faction of Nvidia’s workforce had demanded his return and greeted him with chants, raucous applause, and hugs at the company’s headquarters.

But other employees were quietly stewing. Several current and former Nvidia staffers had viewed Huang’s abrupt exit earlier this month as a rare opportunity to change the “one team” corporate culture of unfettered unity and minimal bureaucracy that he had cultivated over the past three decades, according to interviews with the workers, as well as internal correspondence and social media posts reviewed by WIRED. Most spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared backlash from colleagues.

Industry observers note that some employees were alarmed by Huang’s alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a subordinate and another with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. But their frustrations extended beyond the CEO’s personal conduct. Current and former workers describe a culture at Nvidia in which allegedly abusive behavior was tolerated and challenging leadership was perceived as discouraged.

Sources indicate that “Everyone agrees that mistakes were made, the question is what we are ready to forgive,” one employee wrote on an internal platform before Huang’s return. “I don’t know how comfortable I’ll be working at a place where such affairs are not taken extremely seriously.”.

Another added, “If Jensen comes back, I’m not doing any HR trainings ever again.”.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a recent development, when Huang returned to Nvidia’s offices in California on Monday, he told employees who greeted him that he would do a better job with his second chance at CEO. (As of Monday afternoon, he had not yet sent a companywide note about his return, as he was still getting his laptop set back up.).

In a recent development, US president Donald Trump mentioned he played a crucial role in convincing Nvidia's board to bring back Huang. A person close to Trump calls him an irreplaceable CEO and states they expect him to exercise better judgment going forward.

Nvidia’s board announced it will continue an independent investigation into whether Huang had been a target of foreign intelligence services and that it will double down on looks to step up corporate governance.

It’s difficult to gauge how widespread dissatisfaction with Huang’s leadership may be at Nvidia. The firm’s emphasis on unity has historically made it difficult for people to openly question his leadership or choices, workers say. “There's only one team at Nvidia,” the chipmaker’s official website declares.

Industry observers note that A public petition campaign known as Stand With Jensen garnered signatures from more than 10,000 Nvidia purported employees, according to its website. Nvidia has roughly 49,000 employees and 18,000 contractors overall, according to a person familiar with its workforce.

But inside Nvidia, one employee told colleagues that “some portion” of the signatures appeared to be “illegitimate,” noting that the names included “Satan” and media personality Mia Khalifa, who does not work at the chipmaker. The employee wrote that they found 75 suspicious names in an hour of checking. WIRED was unable to independently verify the findings. The petition’s organizers did not respond to requests for comment.

Industry observers note that huang’s supporters have praised how he made the tech giant feel like a “major super family.” They credited him for minimizing bureaucracy, making himself available to staff, and supporting employees during difficult periods, including the Covid pandemic. A former employee who attended numerous meetings with Huang and other senior executives says the CEO was particularly adept at preventing bureaucratic infighting. He could detect corporate “politics and nonsense before it was even born,” says the worker.

In a recent development, there are also powerful financial reasons for Nvidia employees to feel loyal to Huang. His bets on chips and software for artificial intelligence have transformed Nvidia into one of the world’s most valuable companies and made many longtime employees wealthy in the process.

Sources indicate that but for some employees, the revelations about Huang’s behavior have forced them to question that loyalty. Jason Sequeira, a longtime engineering leader at Nvidia, wrote on LinkedIn last week that he ultimately couldn’t decide whether he wanted Huang back as he weighed arguments from both sides. “Some believe his contributions to Nvidia and the industry are so extraordinary that he deserves another chance,” Sequeira wrote. “Others argue that making exceptions for powerful leaders sets a dangerous precedent. … I don’t have a clear answer.”.

In a recent development, several current and former workers say that Huang’s management style could come off as overly harsh at times, including, for example, toward longtime colleagues he viewed as having grown complacent as Nvidia’s market value surged. Two former employees say that he regularly raised his voice at workers, sometimes in ways they found belittling.

Other employees were more concerned about whether Nvidia’s board would hold Huang accountable for allegedly misleading the directors about his affairs. “That’s something we can’t have,” one employee indicates.

Recent findings suggest that another source of frustration for Nvidia workers has been the growing influence of Huang’s two children and son-in-law, who all hold senior titles at the chipmaker. In March, his daughter, Madison Huang, scolded a colleague on a call with about 100 other employees, according to a participant who didn’t believe the anger was warranted. “I’m disappointed you asked that. Are you fucking stupid?” the employee recalls Madison saying in response to a question about workshops on OpenClaw technology scheduled for an upcoming Nvidia conference. “Your mom can build a claw.”.

Madison and her brother, Spencer Huang, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Praveen Mhapsekar, a senior system software engineer who separated with Nvidia last week after disputes with his managers and HR, indicates he and colleagues stopped feeling comfortable complaining about practices that concerned them because of the trouble they believe it brought on themselves.

Recent findings suggest that “This organization requires greater discipline and structured processes,” he says. One of the world’s most valuable companies “cannot be managed like a private startup operating out of a garage, where personal influence takes precedence over established procedures.”.

It has been revealed that huang’s return doesn’t eliminate the prospect of Nvidia evolving to quell frustrations. But with internal challenges more public than ever before, maybe the days of one massive family all cheering along together are mostly gone.

Additional reporting by Lauren Goode and Hugo Lowell.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 24) that AI-generated music will be banned entirely from the platform, beginning Dec.
  • Industry observers note that in a post on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter), Tidal claimed that 94% of AI-badged tracks had come from Suno.
  • “If you make music, you should be able to put it on Tidal knowing it won’t be buried under tracks no one asked for, or copied by someone pretending to be you,” the blog post read.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tidal announced Tuesday (Nov. 24) that AI-generated music will be banned entirely from the platform, beginning Dec. 9. This follows the company’s announcement in July that AI music had been demonetized and labeled, with requirements for distributors to label AI songs. Tidal states that it will remove any songs that distributors say were created solely with AI tools.

Industry observers note that in a post on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter), Tidal claimed that 94% of AI-badged tracks had come from Suno. The company also claimed in a blog post that as of Nov. 6, 60% of the songs that it had received daily were AI-generated, that 96% of AI-generated songs on its platform had received no streams over the last three months and that it had taken down 66,000 tracks from people it suspects are impersonating another artist. The company indicates that songs created with assistance from AI tools, but are not entirely AI-generated, will be allowed to remain on the platform.

“If you make music, you should be able to put it on Tidal knowing it won’t be buried under tracks no one asked for, or copied by someone pretending to be you,” the blog post read.

Tidal’s statement also stated that 43% of songs delivered to the platform over the last three months have been marked as AI and labeled with a badge. Labeling has been a significant part of the push to regulate AI music across platforms. This summer, a coalition of record labels got together to propose a newly introduced system for tagging AI-generated songs on streaming services and called on those platforms to adopt it. So far, none of them have adopted that exact proposal, but services like Tidal, Spotify, Deezer and Apple Music all created some form of a system on their own.

In a recent development, tidal is the first streaming service to outright ban AI songs from its platform. It joins online record store service BandCamp and radio company iHeartRadio as the only firms placing a full prohibition on fully AI works. Other sites like Deezer, Spotify and Apple Music have explored solutions that fall short of a total ban. Commonly, services will try labeling AI music, regulating spam and fraud associated with it or removing it from recommendation engines, rather than resorting to a full ban.

Just last week, SoundCloud announced a upcoming policy update to better tackle harmful side effects of AI music, like spam, impersonation and streaming fraud. The platform, however, has taken a much more flexible stance toward AI than other services. SoundCloud recently formed partnerships with AI companies Moises and ElevenLabs to allow a direct pipeline for those generated songs from those trusted partners to be shared on SoundCloud.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, both services make songs based on fully licensed training data and have large support within the music business. “Simply wishing away the advent of AI music is not a strategy,” SoundCloud CEO Eliah Seton told Billboard about the newly introduced policy enhancement. “There’s been a very binary frame: [AI music] is either good or evil, accept it or reject it…it’s high time we changed the frame from something so binary and reductive to include the nuance that artists deserve.”.

Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hydrogen flames can glow bright orange one day and become almost impossible to see the next, even when the burner settings remain exactly the same.
  • The study, published in Next Energy, found that much of the difference comes down to sodium, a naturally occurring element carried through the air in microscopic particles.
  • It has been revealed that when sodium is present in the surrounding air, hydrogen flames can take on a noticeable orange glow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hydrogen flames can glow bright orange one day and become almost impossible to see the next, even when the burner settings remain exactly the same. Researchers at Adelaide University have now identified a surprising reason for this dramatic change, offering insights that could help make hydrogen-powered stoves, ovens, and other household appliances safer and more dependable.

The study, published in Next Energy, found that much of the difference comes down to sodium, a naturally occurring element carried through the air in microscopic particles. Sea salt transported inland by the wind is one crucial source.

It has been revealed that when sodium is present in the surrounding air, hydrogen flames can take on a noticeable orange glow. But when sodium concentrations fall, the flames become much harder to see, even though the burner continues operating under the same conditions.

This discovery has key implications for the development of hydrogen appliances. Instead of depending on flame color to show whether a burner is running, engineers may need to incorporate other detection technologies. Improving these systems could help support the adoption of hydrogen as a lower-emissions alternative to natural gas.

Why Hydrogen Flames Change Color With the Weather.

Lead researcher Professor Paul Medwell, from the School of Electrical and Mechanical Engineering at Adelaide University, explained that studying hydrogen flames under ordinary environmental conditions is essential for developing appliances that people can safely and confidently use at home.*.

"Hydrogen has significant potential as part of a lower-emissions energy future, and we need to understand how it behaves in the real world if we want people to be confident using it.

"Our research helps explain why hydrogen flames can look different from one day to the next. That knowledge gives engineers valuable information to develop appliances and flame-detection systems that work reliably, regardless of changing environmental conditions.".

To investigate these changes, the researchers combined controlled laboratory experiments with outdoor testing around Adelaide. They examined how hydrogen flames responded to variations in atmospheric conditions, including shifting weather patterns and changes in the air reaching the burner.

Over two weeks, the team monitored light emissions from hydrogen flames while keeping the burner settings unchanged. Despite the consistent operating conditions, the sodium-related light signal varied by more than 28 times between its lowest and highest recorded values.

Weather played a major role in those differences. Air that had passed over the ocean generally contained more sodium, producing flames with a stronger orange glow. When the air carried less sodium, the flames appeared considerably fainter.

Hydrogen Flames Are Harder to See Than Natural Gas Flames.

The researchers also examined how hydrogen flames compared with those produced by a conventional natural gas cooktop.

According to recent reports, they found that hydrogen flames emitted less visible light on average, even when atmospheric conditions favored a brighter flame. This difference presents an additional challenge for appliances that use visible flames to indicate whether a burner is operating.

It has been revealed that hydrogen combustion can also produce faint blue and red light. However, the researchers found that these colors were easiest to detect in darkened surroundings, making them less useful as reliable visual indicators under everyday lighting conditions.

Together, the findings show why judging whether a hydrogen burner is operating based on appearance alone may be unreliable. A flame that is clearly visible under one set of conditions could become extremely difficult to detect when the surrounding air changes.

Making Hydrogen-Powered Homes Safer.

Medwell emphasized that the results do not undermine hydrogen's potential as an energy source. Instead, they demonstrate why appliances must be engineered to accommodate the fuel's particular properties.

"Different energy sources have different properties, and good engineering is about understanding those differences and designing for them.

Recent findings suggest that "Rather than relying on a flame looking a particular color, we can investigate other ways of confirming that a burner is operating. Options include specialized ultraviolet or infrared flame detectors and temperature sensors.

"By identifying the factors that influence flame visibility, we can help inform the development of hydrogen appliances that are fit for purpose in real homes and other everyday settings.".

Such detection systems could provide a more dependable way to confirm that hydrogen is burning, regardless of whether its flame appears orange, faint blue, or is barely visible.

By identifying how environmental sodium affects flame visibility, the research provides information that engineers can use when designing hydrogen appliances for kitchens and other everyday environments. That knowledge could help make the technology safer and more practical as interest in lower-emissions energy alternatives grows.

The project brought together researchers from Adelaide University, the University of Newly introduced South Wales, and Gas Infrastructure Research Australia. Support came through the Future Fuels Cooperative Research Centre, with funding provided under the Australian Government's Cooperative Research Centres Program.

The study, 'The role of sodium on hydrogen flame visibility in domestic settings,' was published in Next Energy.

It has been revealed that *In 2023, the Australian Gas Infrastructure Group (AGIG) introduced Australia's first 100% hydrogen-powered home in Victoria. The demonstration indicated that household gas appliances could operate entirely on hydrogen, a development described as a 'game changer'.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, amazon's first satellite launch since a rocket failure that doomed 40 of its spacecraft went off without a hitch Tuesday morning (Nov. 24).

According to recent reports, an Ariane 6 rocket carrying 36 satellites for the Amazon Leo constellation lifted off at 6:14 a.m. EST (1114 GMT) from Europe's Spaceport in Kourou, French Guiana, on Tuesday (Nov. 23), right at the end of the 29-minute window that opened at 6:45 a.m. EST (1045 GMT; 7:45 a.m. local time in Kourou).

Sources indicate that the launch was originally supposed to take place on Monday (Nov. 23), but that attempt was scrubbed due to a technical matter affecting the rocket's ground support systems, according to Arianespace.

Amazon Leo, so named because it will operate in low Earth orbit, will compete with SpaceX's Starlink internet constellation, which currently consists of more than 11,000 operational spacecraft.

Sources indicate that amazon's network will eventually have more than 3,200 satellites, but just 400 or so have reached orbit to date. Another 40 were supposed to be delivered on Nov. 15, but they were lost after their rocket ride, a United Launch Alliance (ULA) Vulcan Centaur, suffered a problem shortly after launch.

Ariane 6 and Vulcan Centaur aren't the only rockets Amazon is depending on to build its broadband constellation. Jeff Bezos' firm has also booked rides on ULA's Atlas V rocket, Blue Origin's Fresh Glenn and SpaceX's Falcon 9.

Recent findings suggest that vulcan will be grounded for a while as ULA investigates the Nov. 15 failure and works to fix whatever caused it. And Newly introduced Glenn hasn't flown since April, when the rocket failed to deliver AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird 7 satellite to the proper orbit. New Glenn's return to flight was further complicated on May 28, when the rocket exploded during a routine prelaunch test.

It has been revealed that the Ariane 6, the successor to Arianespace's Ariane 5 heavy lifter, debuted in July 2024 and has nine launches under its belt to date. All of them have been successful except that maiden mission, which was a partial failure.

This morning's launch was the fourth Amazon Leo flight for the Ariane 6, following releases in February, April and June of this year.
